Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies on the Firing Line, or Twelve Days Battle Along the Marne. The A. L. Burt Company of New York put it out, with rights dated 1915. The first chapter is called Terrible Odds. Hal Paine and Chester Crawford ride with a small body of British troopers.

Chester says it feels good to be back at work, and Hal agrees with warmth. The party counts just forty-eight men in all. The two boys ride as guides, ten miles in front of the main host, along the river Marne. For hours they ride slow and meet no foe. Then the troop tops a small hill, and the plain below comes into view. Hal pulls up his horse with a cry, throws up his right hand, and the whole troop halts at once.
the-boy-aviators-treasure-quest-or-the-g: Captain Wilbur Lawton wrote The Boy Aviators' Treasure Quest, or The Golden Galleon. A note says Lawton is a pen name for John Henry Goldfrap. The book is fourth in his Boy Aviators set of six cloth books at fifty cents each. The first chapters here are The Eagle and the Buzzard, Billy's Strange Tale, and A Trial Flight. Eben Joyce Appears and A Strange Story come next, and the list stops there.
the-boy-scouts-of-the-flying-squadron:
Scout Master Robert Shaler wrote The Boy Scouts of the Flying Squadron. Its chapters pair two Wolf Patrol boys with a camp supper, a strange blast, and a sign read by torchlight. A fool-proof aeroplane, a red letter day in the woods, and Bud's meteor come next. Uncle Sam's Flying Squadron and a ride in a war monoplane close the list, with foreign spies sent off.

The first chapter finds Bud Morgan and Hugh worn out on the frozen side of old Stormberg mountain. Both boys own they are near done in, with hard going and heavy packs to blame. A big Thanksgiving meal sits oddly with such a trek. A lift from Farmer Badgely, home from market, put miles behind them. Their goal is a shanty by nightfall. Hugh calls the halt over, Bud heaves his pack onto his back, and the two set off once more.
the-boys-of-columbia-high-on-the-gridiro: Graham B. Forbes wrote The Boys of Columbia High on the Gridiron, or The Struggle for the Silver Cup. A plate shows Coots downed by a fierce tackle from Shadduck. The chapters start Out for Practice, then take to the road to town. The Strange History of Ralph and Treachery in the Camp come next. Signal practice and the kidnap of Bones lead to the line-up with Clifford. Dr. Shadduck's fear of sickness closes the heads shown.
the-brotherhood-of-consolation:
Honore de Balzac wrote The Brotherhood of Consolation, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. Its first episode is Madame de la Chanterie, and its first part The Malady of the Age. On a fine September evening in 1836, a man of about thirty leans on the parapet of a quay. From there a viewer can look up the Seine from the Jardin des Plantes to Notre-Dame, and down to the Louvre.

Balzac calls the spot the quarter-deck of a gigantic vessel. From it Paris dreams itself from the Romans to Louis-Philippe. The cupola of Sainte-Geneviève towers over the Latin quarter, and the cathedral's apse rises behind. Below lie the rags of a foul nest of houses by the quai de la Tournelle. Between viewer and cathedral spreads the Terrain, still strewn with the ruins of the Archiepiscopal Palace.
the-caged-lion:
The Caged Lion opens with a preface, transcribed from the Macmillan edition of 1912, in which its author owns what liberties were taken with history. No author's name is printed in these pages. The tale deals with Henry V and his prisoner, James I of Scotland. The imprisonment sheltered him, in his youth, from the violence of his own nobles.

James's expedition to Scotland is wholly imaginary, the preface grants, though room for it lay in Henry's progress north to Beverley Minster. The hero, Malcolm, is invention too, cast as a son of one of King Robert II's eleven sons who loved arms. The preface names its sources: Tyler's Henry V, Strickland's Queens, Tytler's Scotland, Barante's history of Burgundy, and Fox Bourne's English Merchants for the Whittington tradition. One anachronism, a knighthood placed some years early, is confessed without apology.
the-call-of-the-canyon:
Zane Grey wrote The Call of the Canyon, a tale in twelve chapters named by number alone. Chapter I opens in New York on a day typical of early April, cold and gray, with women in furs along Fifty-seventh Street. Glenn has been gone over a year, three months over. This letter of his seems the strangest of all. She lives again their last moments, on New-Year's Eve, 1918, at the McAlpin, in a suite high up on the twenty-first floor, with Broadway below.

Glenn Kilbourne had come back from France that fall, shell-shocked and gassed, a wreck of his former self, and in many ways a stranger to her. Cold, silent, and haunted, he had made her miserable with his aloofness. As the bells rang out the year that had been his ruin, he drew her close at the open window.
the-chaperon:
A tale of two mourners opens in a high London drawing room thick with fog. An old lady in deep mourning sits close to the fire, knitting, her chair drawn near the warmth. Her face holds a faded nobleness, though her lips press tight with some train of thought she is working through.

A girl of twenty enters, also in fresh mourning, holding a sealed and addressed letter. Her arrival, the telling notes, feeds the old lady's thoughts rather than breaking them. The girl rings for the butler and asks that the letter be posted, then drifts about the room in silence. She gives her grandmother, for such the elder proves to be, the chance to speak first. Both hold out, and the strain grows, until the old lady yields a trifle grudgingly. Fine social pressure, watched at close range, drives the scene.
the-chemistry-of-food-and-nutrition: A. W. Duncan, F.C.S., an analytical chemist of Manchester, wrote this work on food and health, issued by the Vegetarian Society in 1905. Only the title page is present here, followed by a full-page advert for Grape-Nuts and Postum Food Coffee, which praises a plain breakfast of cooked fruit, cereal, eggs, and toast.A title page and a contents list are all that stand here.
the-children-s-portion: Robert W. Shoppell selected and edited these entertaining and elevating stories for children, published by The Christian Herald at the Bible House in New York, copyrighted in 1895 by Louis Klopsch. Only the title page and contents are present here. The tales include work by Agnes Strickland, the Grimm Brothers, and pieces drawn from Chaucer, such as Pious Constance and Patient Griselda. The first story, The Golden Age by the Rev. Alexander McLeod, is named at the end, but no story text follows.
the-circassian-slave-or-the-sultan-s-fav:
Lieutenant Murray wrote this novelette of Constantinople and the Caucasus, published at Boston in 1851. A publisher's note says it first ran in the Pictorial Drawing Room Companion, a popular journal praised for its corps of contributors. The contents promise a slave market, a sultan's harem, a slave ship, and an escape.

The preface places the tale in a romantic borderland: the shores of the Black Sea, the Sea of Marmora, and the Bosphorus. Its period is quite modern, and its scenes claim to mirror present life in the city. Chapter titles then map the plot in bold strokes: the sultan's prisoner, the punishment of the sack, a lover's stratagem, a serenade, an elopement, and a struggle for life. The chase ends, the list promises, in a happy conclusion. Readers get a period melodrama of captivity and love in the Ottoman world.
the-clarion: Samuel Hopkins Adams wrote this novel, published in October 1914 with pictures by W. D. Stevens, and inscribed it to the memory of his father Myron Adams, called a soldier of ideals. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here. The chapters name an itinerant, a leading citizen, the shop, the scion, and the owner.Its contents rest on the strength of the title page alone.
the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-html-:
Charles Farrar Browne wrote as Artemus Ward, and this complete works gathering opens with a table of contents and a biographical sketch by Melville D. Landon. Part I is given to essays, sketches, and letters. The titles show Ward's range across American humor in his own day.

Early pieces include Mr. Ward's first business letter, a piece on forts, the Shakers, and a high-handed outrage at Utica. Show business runs through the list: the showman's courtship, wax figures against Shakspeare, and the show business and popular lectures. Public life enters too, with an interview with President Lincoln, a visit to Brigham Young, Ossawatomie Brown, and a piece on how Old Abe received the news of his nomination. Woman's rights, the Atlantic cable, and a celebration at Baldinsville also appear.
the-confession:
Mary Roberts Rinehart opens this tale with a narrator who distrusts her own impressions. She is not a susceptible woman, she says, being objective rather than subjective. A full experience of life has taught her that most of her impressions run from within outward, not the other way.

She gives cases. An obsession with a shadowy figure on her right, just past her field of vision, proved to be a defect in her glasses. Her old servant Maggie was haunted one whole summer by church bells, a personal summons to eternity, until the cause was found in her inner ear. Yet the Benton house, she insists, undeniably made her uncomfortable. It had stayed unchanged for years: horsehair chairs in shiny mahogany frames had worn the carpet bare in fixed spots before them.
the-correspondence-of-thomas-carlyle-and: Volume I of the correspondence between Thomas Carlyle and Ralph Waldo Emerson covers the years 1834 to 1872. Lines from each man head the volume, with the matter signed by Charles Eliot Norton at Cambridge, Massachusetts, on January 29, 1883. A note to the revised edition reports that thirteen lost letters of Carlyle and four of Emerson have been found since the first printing. Rough drafts of one or two of Emerson's letters, whose sent copies went astray, have also turned up. Only the front matter and that note are present here.
the-covered-wagon: Emerson Hough, author of Heart's Desire, wrote The Covered Wagon, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap and dated 1922, with pictures from the Paramount photoplay of the same name. A photograph at the front shows Hough himself driving a covered wagon. The contents open with chapters called Youth Marches, The Edge of the World, The Rendezvous, Fever of New Fortunes, The Black Spaniard, Issue Joined, and The Jump-Off. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here.
the-craft-of-fiction:
Percy Lubbock published The Craft of Fiction with Jonathan Cape of London in 1921. He opens on the critic's core problem: a book will not hold still. To grasp its shape and survey it at leisure is the critic's aim. Yet the effort is always defeated, since a book melts and shifts in memory as fast as it is read.

By the last page, Lubbock says, much of a book's fine detail is already vague, and a few days later only a cluster of impressions stays behind. No one would judge a building or a statue from one passing glimpse, yet the critic of books must found his view on little more. Of the hundreds of books he would hold in mind for calm comparison, few can be brought to any firm stability.
the-critique-of-practical-reason:
Immanuel Kant's Critique of Practical Reason, dated 1788 and translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, opens with a preface explaining its title. Kant says the book critiques practical reason as a whole, not pure practical reason alone, though its parallel with the speculative critique might suggest the longer name.

Its business, he writes, is to show that pure practical reason exists. If reason, as pure, is truly practical, it proves its own reality by fact, and arguing against its possibility is futile. With this faculty, he argues, freedom in the absolute sense stands firm too: speculative reason could only hold freedom as a thought not proven impossible, while the moral law proves it real. Freedom thus becomes the keystone of the whole system, giving the ideas of God and immortality their support.
the-death-of-the-lion:
Henry James's The Death of the Lion appears here in the Martin Secker edition first published in London in 1915, the text following the Definitive Edition. Chapter I opens on a young journalist explaining a change of heart that began when Mr. Pinhorn sent his manuscript back.

Pinhorn is his chief at a weekly paper he was hired to bring up, a paper nearly past redemption under its late owner-editor, Mr. Deedy. The narrator was taken over with the office plant and furniture when the widowed Mrs. Deedy sold out, and he half resents the blame heaped on his dead protector. Aware he is suspected as a product of the old, flat system, he feels doubly bound to have ideas. So he proposed to Pinhorn that he should lay his lean hands on the celebrity Neil Paraday.
the-dominion-of-the-air-the-story-of-aer:
Rev. J. M. Bacon's The Dominion of the Air tells the story of flight from myth to balloons. Chapter one, The Dawn of Aeronautics, quotes Bishop Wilkins on learning to fly from youth, then notes that even he borrowed from older men. It cites Archytas and his flying wooden pigeon, and a man in Nero's Rome who flew high and died.

Bacon sorts true trials from tall tales with care and humour. Later chapters reach kites, balloons, and airships. The book catches the mood just before powered flight, when the air still seemed a sea to be sailed.
the-double-life-of-mr-alfred-burton: E. Phillips Oppenheim's The Double Life of Mr. Alfred Burton, dated 1913 in its front pages, is present here only as a title page and a thirty-chapter contents list. First titles name the fruit of a tree and a transformation. Later ones name Menatogen, the mind food, and the real Alfred Burton. No story text appears. The list alone hints at a clerk remade by a strange food.
the-duke-of-stockbridge-a-romance-of-sha:
Edward Bellamy's The Duke of Stockbridge, a romance of Shays' Rebellion, opens on August 17, 1777, as dawn strikes the Housatonic valley. Bellamy paints the village in its changeless frame of hills, lakes, and brooks, then notes how little a modern eye would know the place itself. The first chapter is named The March of the Minute Men.

War debt and hard tax drove poor farmers to revolt in 1786. Bellamy, famed for a utopia tale, here traces class strife at the nation's birth. A proud poor man leads his neighbours against rich creditors.
the-dynasts-an-epic-drama-of-the-war-wit:
Thomas Hardy's The Dynasts is an epic drama of the war with Napoleon, built in three parts, nineteen acts, and one hundred and thirty scenes across some ten years. Hardy's preface traces the work to his home ground: the coast near George the Third's summer seat, thick with invasion scares, and the village that bore Nelson's flag-captain at Trafalgar.

Spirits watch kings and crowds as Europe burns. Hardy had first touched the theme in The Trumpet Major. The vast verse play asks if men steer history or a blind will steers them.
the-early-poems-of-alfred-lord-tennyson:
John Churton Collins edited The Early Poems of Alfred Lord Tennyson with a long critical preface, notes, variant readings, and a bibliography. Collins argues that Tennyson's growth can be traced with rare fullness in these poems. The path runs from the 1830 Poems, Chiefly Lyrical, writ before his twenty-second year. It runs through 1832. It ends at the famed 1842 volumes. Those won him first place among living poets.

Suppressed poems are printed too, with their variants. Collins names the 1830 set piece by piece, from Claribel and Lilian on. Scholars still use his notes to watch a great poet form.
the-earth-as-modified-by-human-action:
George P. Marsh's The Earth as Modified by Human Action, a new edition of Man and Nature dated 1874, states its aim in the first preface. Marsh means to show how much human hands have changed the globe, to warn against rash works that break nature's order, and to urge the mending of waste and worn-out lands.

Man, he holds, is a power of a higher order than any beast. Marsh counts felled woods, drained marshes, and worn soils across the old world. The book stands at the root of the modern green movement.
the-eldest-son:
John Galsworthy's play The Eldest Son, first of his second series of plays, lists the Cheshire family at the front. Sir William and Lady Cheshire head a house of three sons' lines and three daughters, with guests, a parson, keepers, and servants. The acts run over December 7 and 8 at their country house in one of the shires.

Bill, the heir, loves Freda, the lady's maid, while young Dunning, the under-keeper, has got a village girl with child. One rule for the rich and one for the poor: Galsworthy sets the two cases side by side.
the-enchanted-canyon:
Honoré Willsie's The Enchanted Canyon, copyrighted in 1921, lays its tale in three books. Book one, Bright Angel, names Minetta Lane; book two jumps twenty-two years and makes its man Secretary of the Interior, with Diana Allen and a photographer of Indians in train. Book three bears the title itself and opens in the desert.

Willsie, who later wrote as Honoré Willsie Morrow, sets love and duty in the Grand Canyon country. A dam scheme for the Colorado pits greed against the canyon's wild worth. Her West glows with heat and colour.
the-end-of-her-honeymoon:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes's The End of Her Honeymoon, dated 1913, opens in Paris near midnight. John Dampier, Nancy's husband of three weeks, calls out their hotel's name to the cabman with glee, then jokes with the driver in French that Nancy cannot catch. He insists on a slow drive by the boulevards: Paris, he says, never sleeps, and she must not see it from an ugly angle first.

Nancy hugs close, thrilled and a touch lost. What waits at the hotel ends the honeymoon in dread. Lowndes builds slow menace from small, off-key notes.
the-eulogies-of-howard-a-vision:
The Eulogies of Howard, a vision dated 1791, mourns John Howard, the prison reformer. Its writer tells how talk with a friend of Howard, just after word of his death reached England, turned to what honours a grateful nation should pay him. The friend held that showy memorials would clash with Howard's meek virtues; the writer hoped for them all the same.

Their split shapes the piece: verse praise set as a dream of fame's court. Howard had died of camp fever while probing plague and prisons abroad. The poem shows how fast the age raised him to a saint of mercy.
the-eve-of-the-french-revolution:
Edward J. Lowell's The Eve of the French Revolution opens by splitting study of the Revolution in two. Most tales rush to the Bastille, the march on Versailles, the September massacres, and the Terror, Lowell says, and skim the calm years before the storm. Such haste breeds glib claims that old France was rotten to the core and her folk all wretches.

Lowell slows down to show taxes, courts, bread prices, and daily grievance as they truly stood. His calm build won praise on both sides of the Atlantic. The book suits readers who want causes, not just drums.
the-extermination-of-the-american-bison:
William T. Hornaday, head of the National Zoological Park, wrote this study for the Smithsonian's National Museum, printed in Washington in 1889. It came out of the museum report for 1886-87 and runs to many pages with plates.

Part one traces the life history of the American bison. Chapters cover how the species was found, where it ranged, how vast the herds once were, and the animal's habits and young. The title states the grim theme plainly: a huge wild herd was being wiped out, and Hornaday set down the record while mounted groups still stood in the museum.
the-eye-of-zeitoon: Talbot Mundy is named on the title page of The Eye of Zeitoon. His past books Rung Ho and King of the Khyber Rifles are listed with it. Only the front matter and part of the contents are present here. The heads that can be read run through fourteen chapters. They speak of Armenia burning and of robbers. They name a squadron under Rustum Khan and a pistol shot. All this points to an adventure tale set in the Near East.
the-facts-of-reconstruction:
John R. Lynch wrote The Facts of Reconstruction, printed in 1913, a first-hand account of how the South was rebuilt after the Civil War. Lynch took part in Mississippi politics, and the contents follow his state step by step.

Early chapters cover the new state offices under Governor Alcorn, the county meeting of 1869, and laws on schools and public life. Later ones tell of B. K. Bruce going to the United States Senate, the fall of the Republican state government, and Lynch's own talk with the President. The book argues from inside the events it records.
the-far-horizon:
Lucas Malet, the pen name of Mrs. Mary St. Leger Harrison, wrote The Far Horizon as a novel of faith and doubt. Verses from Jeremiah and from Lao-Tzu stand at the front, along with a passage from Flaubert.

Those mottoes set the book's ground: an old path to walk in, a good man teaching a bad one, and art drawn from any stuff of life. Malet, author of The History of Sir Richard Calmady, was known for grave tales of moral strain. Here the pull between worldly success and the claims of the soul shapes the lives the novel follows.
the-father-of-british-canada-a-chronicle:
William Wood wrote The Father of British Canada as volume twelve of the Chronicles of Canada, printed at Toronto in 1916. Guy Carleton, first Baron Dorchester, stands at the center of the tale.

Carleton was born at Strabane on September 3, 1724, and got his first army post at eighteen. The chapters follow him as soldier, governor, and defender of Quebec. He beats back the invasion of 1776, guards the Loyalists after the war, and helps found modern Canada. Wood shows how one calm, firm man held a new land for the Crown and shaped its laws.
the-fight-for-conservation:
Gifford Pinchot wrote The Fight for Conservation in 1910 to state the case for saving America's woods, waters, and soil. Twelve short chapters build the plea, from prosperity to what he calls the present battle.

Pinchot opens with a claim: the land's wealth rests on its rich natural stores, and those stores will not last if wasted. He asks if the nation will hand them down unspent, or leave want and decay to its children. Chapters on farms, waterways, business, and morals frame conservation as a duty owed to all, with an equal chance for each child of the republic.
the-flying-legion: George Allan England wrote The Flying Legion as an air adventure tale, printed in July 1920. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The heads name a caged spirit and a masked recruit. They name a great bird's nest and an eagle of the sky. A French ace named Leclair stands in the list. A scourge of flame closes it. All this points to a tale of a secret band of airmen on a bold raid. No chapter text can be read in this opening portion.
the-forgotten-threshold-a-journal-of-art:
Arthur Middleton left this journal, The Forgotten Threshold, and a friend prints part of it after his death. The editor gives the book to W. S. B. and adds a note on what was left out.

The editor says Middleton could never speak his inmost thoughts in life, though his eyes showed a dream that ate his heart. Only the most private parts were cut. Middleton, of the old Catholic faith, would have owned full loyalty to the Roman Church. The journal starts with a scrap of memoir: a child of three made glad by sunlight through curtains, a joy that grew into a hunt for light in all things.
the-four-million:
O. Henry gathered twenty-five tales in The Four Million, his famed set of New York sketches. The Gift of the Magi stands second in the contents, among tales of cops, clerks, and cabbies.

The first tale, Tobin's Palm, opens with two men off to Coney Island with four dollars between them. Tobin's sweetheart Katie has been lost since she sailed from Ireland with his savings and her own. A palm reading at the shore starts the hunt. Through the set, O. Henry finds plot twists in furnished rooms, cafes, and park benches, where the city's four million live their small, sharp lives.
the-galleries-of-the-exposition:
Eugen Neuhaus wrote The Galleries of the Exposition as a critical review of the art in the Palace of Fine Arts at the Panama-Pacific Fair in San Francisco. Neuhaus taught design at the University of California and sat on the fair's jury of awards.

The book works nation by nation: France, Italy, Portugal, the South American states, Cuba, the Philippines, Japan, China, and the lands of northern Europe. A long part treats the United States, with whole rooms given to Whistler, Sargent, Chase, Hassam, and others. Neuhaus sorts the fair's vast show into schools and hands, judging what each land sent to the great fair of 1915.
the-girl-and-her-religion: Margaret Slattery wrote The Girl and Her Religion. The Pilgrim Press printed it in Boston. Its copyright is dated 1913. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a short note, and the contents. Slattery says the book is plain and concrete. She asks readers to think about girls, not about her. The contents name types of girls. They run from the handicapped girl and the girl who drifts to the girl with high ideals. Later heads turn to faith, the universe, and rules of right and wrong.
the-glimpses-of-the-moon:
Edith Wharton wrote The Glimpses of the Moon. Part I opens on a honeymoon by an Italian lake. The lake is famed for romance. Susy Lansing and her husband Nick stand on a marble terrace. They watch the moon lay a bright path across the water.

The pair joke about their choice of spot. It took a lack of humor, or a great gift of it, to risk it. They count the houses lent to them by rich friends. There is Strefford's villa, a place at Versailles, and a villa at Monte Carlo. There is also a moor. Their gay talk hides a plain fact. They are poor, married for love, and living on the kindness of the rich. The novel will test that bargain.
the-glory-of-english-prose-letters-to-my: The Hon. Stephen Coleridge wrote The Glory of English Prose. Its subtitle is Letters to My Grandson. G. P. Putnam's Sons printed it in New York and London in 1922. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of twenty letters. The letters treat style and the glory of the Bible. They then treat English writers: Raleigh, Hooker, Browne, Milton, Taylor, Bunyan, Johnson, Burke, and Gibbon. Dr. Johnson gives the motto: a people's chief glory arises from its authors.
the-god-idea-of-the-ancients-or-sex-in-r:
Eliza Burt Gamble wrote The God-Idea of the Ancients. Its subtitle is Or Sex in Religion. Gamble also wrote The Evolution of Woman. Her preface explains the book's roots. Much of the matter was gathered during work on that earlier book. She held this part back for a time. She wanted more facts on the roots of belief and worship.

Gamble argues that people make their own gods. Ideas of the unknown mirror the inner life of those who hold them. A true history of faiths must match the growth of mind, morals, and society. She finds a fresh chain of proof in the data. Sex, she argues, lies at the root of how thought split into two lines. She builds her case on that ground.
the-gold-hunters-a-story-of-life-and-adv:
James Oliver Curwood wrote The Gold Hunters. Its subtitle is A Story of Life and Adventure in the Hudson Bay Wilds. The book is dated 1909. Curwood dedicates it to a half-Cree maiden at Lac-Bain. She is the Minnetaki of the tale. He also honors Teddy Brown, guide and trapper, his comrade on many trips. Chapter I is called The Pursuit of the Hudson Bay Mail.

The chapter opens at noon in the Canadian forest. It is February, and a deep hush lies over the solitude. Moose and caribou rest after feeding. The lynx sleeps between rocks, and the fox takes his midday nap. The sun starts to melt late winter snow. Curwood notes the old hunter's noon halt: a fire, a meal, a pipe, and ears kept sharp. Game may lie close by. That still, watchful world is where the gold hunt plays out.
the-golden-canyon: G. A. Henty wrote The Golden Canyon. Hurst and Company printed it in New York in 1899. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of sixteen chapters. The heads run from A Run Ashore and Dick's Escape. They run through The Gold-Seekers and The Search for the Canyon. They name The Scarcity of Water and The Golden Valley. Later heads name Watched, Retreat, The Redskin, and Rifle-Shots. The list points to a western tale of a hunt for a gold canyon.
the-golden-scorpion: Sax Rohmer wrote The Golden Scorpion. Its heading is dated 1919. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a full contents list in four parts. Part I is The Cowled Man. It names a sealed envelope, an assistant commissioner, a Chinese coin, and a blue ray. Part II gives the statement of Gaston Max, with a grand duke and a cafe fight. Part III, At the House of Ah-Fang-Fu, names brain-thieves and an opium den. Part IV is The Lair of the Scorpion.
the-good-resolution:
The Good Resolution was revised by D. P. Kidder. It was printed in 1831 for the Sunday-School Union of the Methodist Episcopal Church. The tale opens on the morning of Isabella Gardner's fourteenth birthday. She wakes unhappy. She asks if the sun is not bright enough, or the flowers not sweet enough. Sunshine lies on the rose bushes at her window.

Isabella dresses and looks ahead to a party that afternoon. Young friends will come to keep her birthday. But she cannot shake her gloom. In her father's garden all is peace. Flowers breathe sweetness, and birds sing with joy. The fault, the tale says, lies within. Isabella has a habit of fretful, peevish temper. She is hasty in her spirit to be angry. A Bible line is quoted against her: anger rests in the bosom of fools. It is a moral tale for girls about ruling one's temper.
the-great-impersonation:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Great Impersonation. It was first published in 1920. Chapter I opens in German East Africa. Everard Dominey has fought his way through the scrub for three quarters of an hour. He follows thin wisps of smoke. He urges his pony to a last effort. He crashes through a great oleander shrub. He pitches forward on his head in a small clearing.

Dominey wakes next morning on a truckle bed between linen sheets. A black boy sits at the entrance of the banda. A tall, slim European in white riding clothes comes to his side. The stranger tells him where he is. He is half a mile from the Iriwarri River. He is seventy-two miles southeast of the Darawaga Settlement. Dominey is stunned. He left Marlinstein two and a half days back. He has ridden into German land, and his host is a German.
the-greater-inclination:
Edith Wharton wrote The Greater Inclination. What is present here is a contents list and the first tale's opening. The contents name eight tales. They are The Muse's Tragedy, A Journey, and The Pelican. They are Souls Belated, A Coward, and The Twilight of the God. They are A Cup of Cold Water and The Portrait.

The Muse's Tragedy opens with Danyers. He likes to fancy that he recognized Mrs. Anerton at once. That, of course, was absurd. He had never seen a portrait of her. She guards her name strictly, and will not let even the most privileged see a photograph of her. From her friend Mrs. Memorall he had drawn one phrase: an old print whose lines have the value of color. He sits over breakfast in an empty hotel restaurant. A lady seats herself near the window. That might be she, he thinks.
the-green-carnation:
Robert Hichens wrote The Green Carnation. D. Appleton and Company published it in New York in 1894. Chapter I opens in a London bedroom on a summer evening. Reggie Hastings slips a green carnation into his evening coat. He fixes it with a pin. He looks at himself in the long glass near the window. He gazes at himself as a woman gazes before a party.

Reggie frankly admires himself. He holds that he is very beautiful, and says so to other people. He keeps only photographs of himself on his mantel-piece. At seven the Sevres clock chimes. He takes lavender gloves from their tissue paper and rings for his valet. A hansom is called to drive to Belgrave Square. That morning his father sent him a long, vehement letter against his way of life. Reggie answered by wire: What a funny little man you are.
the-hallam-succession: Amelia E. Barr wrote The Hallam Succession, and she is named on the title page as the author of Jan Vedder's Wife, The Bow of Orange Ribbon, and Friend Olivia. Contents headings trace a family story through Americans in Yorkshire, Martha Craven's Trouble, Wesley and Methodism, Antony and His Bride, The Squire's Death, Texas and Liberty, and Elizabeth in Texas. The pages present go no further than the front matter.
the-harlequinade-an-excursion:
Dion Clayton Calthrop and Granville Barker wrote The Harlequinade, subtitled an excursion, published in March 1918. A short opening address tells the reader plainly that the piece is not a play, a novel, a treatise, or an essay. Readers are cast as trippers on an outing, sure to fall into talk with odd company.

The address links the trip to the old stage figures Harlequin, Columbine, Clown, and Pantaloon. Sentiment, clownish fun, and wise chuckles are promised in one mix. The writers claim a long line behind them, from Greek and Roman times through medieval Italy and France, and they recall childhood games and sounds to set the tone.
the-hated-son:
Honore de Balzac wrote The Hated Son, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. Part one, How the Mother Lived, opens in a bedroom of the sixteenth century. On a winter night at about two in the morning, the Comtesse Jeanne d'Herouville feels the pains of a first birth drawing near, and she fears dangers that await her child.

The countess rises with extreme care so she will not wake her sleeping husband. Each rustle of the green silk coverlet stops her, and she watches his face as a prisoner might watch a guard. Balzac turns a quiet room into a scene of dread, built from small sounds, held breath, and a mother's need to move unseen.
the-head-hunters-of-northern-luzon: Cornelis De Witt Willcox, a lieutenant-colonel in the U.S. Army and a professor at the United States Military Academy, wrote The Head Hunters of Northern Luzon, published at Kansas City in 1912. The subtitle describes a ride through the mountains of northern Luzon, from Ifugao to Kalinga, with an appendix on Philippine independence. Contents chapters cover the meaning of the word Igorrote, the Mountain Province, and the annual inspection of the mountain tribes. No text past the front matter is present here.
the-history-of-a-lie-the-protocols-of-th:
Herman Bernstein wrote The History of a Lie, a study of The Protocols of the Wise Men of Zion, copyright 1921. He is named as the author of With Master Minds. A foreword calls the Protocols a cruel and terrible lie invented to defame the entire Jewish people, first given out as fiction by a German anti-Semitic writer hiding behind an English pen-name.

The foreword traces what came next. The fiction was changed and dressed up as fact over time. Agents of the Russian secret police and of the Black Hundreds then used it as a frame to crush the Jews and prop up a tottering Russian dynasty. Bernstein sets out to show how a forgery was built and spread.
the-history-of-england-a-study-in-politi:
A. F. Pollard, M.A., Litt.D., wrote The History of England, subtitled a study in political evolution. The contents list nine chapters running from The Foundations of England, 55 B.C. to A.D. 1066, through The Industrial Revolution to English Democracy, plus a chronological table, bibliography, and index. Chapter one opens at the site of the battle of Hastings.

An American visitor is quoted musing that England is but a little island, and often conquered. Pollard sets out to trace how a great empire grew from that island. Readers, he says, now want history as an interpretation of human development, not a bare list of facts and dates, and he credits English growth to powers of assimilation and adaptation.
the-history-of-london: Walter Besant wrote The History of London, shown in a second edition printed in London by Longmans, Green, and Co. in 1894, with a heading in the record dated 1894. Besant is named as the author of London and Children of Gibeon. The contents list numbered lessons with page numbers, starting with The Foundation of London in two lessons, then Roman London in two lessons. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, so the lessons themselves do not appear.
the-history-of-rome-book-iv-the-revoluti: Theodor Mommsen wrote The History of Rome, Book IV, subtitled The Revolution, translated with the author's sanction by William Purdie Dickson, D.D., LL.D., professor of divinity in the University of Glasgow. The German original is named as Roemische Geschichte, Viertes Buch: Die Revolution. Only the title page and a preparer's note on marking foreign words, sounds, and letters in plain text are present here, so the history itself does not appear.
the-history-of-samuel-titmarsh-and-the-g:
The History of Samuel Titmarsh and the Great Hoggarty Diamond is shown in the 1911 John Murray edition, printed in London. No author is named in the pages present. Chapter one gives an account of the narrator's village and the first glimpse of the diamond. Samuel recalls coming up to town for his second year.

His aunt Hoggarty gave him a large old-fashioned locket of Dublin make from 1795, worn by the late Mr. Hoggarty at the Lord Lieutenant's balls and at the battle of Vinegar Hill. Village life, whist and cribbage at his aunt's house, sour black-currant wine he dared not refuse, and hopes raised by her favor fill the opening. The locket is not yet a diamond-pin, yet its story has begun.
the-history-of-sir-richard-whittington:
The History of Sir Richard Whittington, by T. H., is shown in the Chap-Books and Folk-Lore Tracts series, edited by G. L. Gomme and H. B. Wheatley and printed in London for the Villon Society in 1885. Henry B. Wheatley edited the tract and wrote an introduction. He calls the tale of Whittington and his Cat a case where a widespread folk-tale was grafted onto the life of a real man.

Wheatley notes that later versions cut the historical matter more and more. The three chief points of the chap-book story, he says, begin with the poor parentage of the hero. Readers get both the popular tale and a scholar's account of how fact and folklore were joined.
the-home-mission:
T. S. Arthur wrote The Home Mission, printed at Boston and Philadelphia in 1853. The contents list tales such as A Vision of Consolation, The Step-Mother, Power of Kindness, Bear and Forbear, The Social Serpent, The Young Mother, Kate's Experiment, and The Evening Prayer. A preface begins the book's argument about where character is formed.

If good or evil impulses that rule a life were traced to their beginnings, Arthur argues, the origin would most often be found in the home of childhood. Impressions made there last as long as existence itself. Home influence, for good or ill, is the mission ground the tales take up, story by story.
the-hudson-three-centuries-of-history-ro: Wallace Bruce wrote this celebration of the Hudson River. The Bryant Union Company issued it in New York. This copy is the Centennial Edition, copyrighted in 1907. A note explains the footers of the original pages. Each page carried poetry or prose as a footer. Those pieces now sit between paragraphs, marked with asterisks. Only the opening pages and contents start are present here. The chapters themselves do not appear. The contents promise three centuries of material. They run from the Half Moon and the discovery onward, through first settlement.
the-invention-of-a-new-religion:
B. H. Chamberlain published this pamphlet in 1912. He was emeritus professor of Japanese at Tokyo's Imperial University. He begins with Voltaire's scorned view of religion. Priests invented religions, the old philosophers held. Modern Japan, Chamberlain argues, proves them half right. A religion is being made there before our eyes. The Japanese call themselves an irreligious people. He quotes Fukuzawa to that effect. Fukuzawa said he lacked a religious nature.

Yet agnostic Japan teaches a sharp lesson, he writes. Religions can be manufactured for a set end. Worldly purposes drive the making here. Mikado-worship and Japan-worship are the new faith. Loyalty and patriotism form its creed. Older materials were sifted and altered for it. A new center of gravity holds them now. The work is still unfinished, he insists. He points readers to Murdoch's History of Japan for the full record.
the-king-of-ireland-s-son:
Padraic Colum tells this Irish wonder tale in a fireside voice. King Connal ruled Ireland and had three sons. The eldest son's mother was dead. No guide restrained him, so he grew wild. The king and his councillor let him have his own way. Riding and hunting filled his whole day. A hound ran at his heel. A hawk sat on his wrist. A brave steed carried him where he listed.

One morning he finds a gray old man on a heap of stones. The man plays cards with himself. One hand wins, then the other. He cheers his good right and his gallant left in turn. The contents promise Fedelma the enchanter's daughter, the King of the Cats, the Sword of Light, the Town of the Red Castle, and Crom Duv's house.
the-lady-and-sada-san-a-sequel-to-the-la:
Frances Little wrote this sequel for the Century Company in 1912. She dedicated it to two fellow wanderers through the Orient. It resumes the letter form of The Lady of the Decoration. The opening letter is written on the high seas in June 1911. Its writer recalls being told to strike the word surprise. She orders it restored at once. She has left Kentucky after nine quiet years at home. She is on her way to Japan again. This time she travels in wifely disobedience to Jack's wishes.

Jack has done something provokingly right, she explains. Two months earlier he left for a place in China. Its ungodly name belongs to the far wilderness. The earlier book's comedy is re-established in a page. A Kentucky voice reports Japan to her cousin Mate. The narrator is now a wife, not a widow. She schemes to follow him east.
the-lady-of-the-decoration:
Frances Little's novel takes the form of letters home. A young Kentucky widow sails for Japan in them. The first letter is dated San Francisco, July 30, 1901. Behold a soldier on the eve of battle, she writes her cousin Mate. She sits in a stuffy hotel room, not daring to stop whistling. A postage stamp could cover her courage. In the morning she sails for the Flowery Kingdom. Watching loving, tearful faces fade with the train felt like death's bitterness.

She is candid about her marriage. She stuck out neglect, humiliations, and anguish to the end. Death's release brought relief she cannot be blamed for feeling. Her cousin shipped her east of Suez on a four years' contract. She will teach kindergarten in a mission school. The lot is absurd for a woman who never missed a Kentucky Derby. Little's comedy and pathos both live in that voice.
the-last-reformation: F. G. Smith, author of works on Daniel and Revelation, organized his church history around a coming final reform. Only the title pages and contents are present here, listing parts on the church in apostolic days, in history, and in prophecy. Chapters move from early corruption through the Reformation and modern sects to a closing chapter on the last reformation itself. The argument and its biblical evidence do not appear in this record.
the-last-secrets-the-final-mysteries-of-:
John Buchan published his survey of recent exploration in September 1923 and dedicated it to Cecil Rawling, an explorer killed at Ypres. His preface calls the first two decades of the century a distinguished era. Many great geographical riddles, he says, had at last been solved.

Buchan also argues that large unknown places have mostly vanished. Future explorers will fill in survey details rather than find forbidden cities or unclimbed great peaks. Readers get a summing up of polar, mountain, and river feats, framed by wonder at what still stays unknown in small things.
the-last-stetson:
John Fox Jr. opens his Kentucky mountain tale inside old Gabe Bunch mill on the Cumberland River. Steve Marcum rests in a dark corner while the boy Isom pours corn into the hopper. Gabe recalls a feud between the Stetson and Lewallen families that once seemed finished.

Rome Stetson beat Jasper Lewallen in a bare fist fight meant to settle who must leave the mountains. Jasper then ran for his gun, and an unknown shot killed him as he turned. Blame stayed split between Rome and Steve, troops came in, and Rome fled downriver with Martha Lewallen.
the-laws-of-etiquette-or-short-rules-and:
A gentleman author published his short rules for conduct in society at Philadelphia in 1836. His preface says he gathered what years of watching good society had taught him, packed into as short a space as he could manage. He admits little in such a book can be fully original.

Chapters in the contents cover good breeding, dress, salutations, drawing room talk, letters, visits, dinner, balls, funerals, servants, and fashion. Promptness gets a chapter of its own. Readers can watch early American manners borrow British forms while praising ease, care, and steady attention to others.
the-life-and-letters-of-lewis-carroll-re: Stuart Dodgson Collingwood wrote the life and letters of his uncle Lewis Carroll, the Reverend C. L. Dodgson, in 1898. Only the title page, dedication, and the start of the contents are present here, listing a first chapter on Carroll forebears, Daresbury, Croft, boyish amusements, and Rugby school. Collingwood dedicates the book to Carroll child friends and to all who love his writings. The biography itself cannot be read in this record.
the-life-of-francis-marion: W. Gilmore Simms wrote his life of Francis Marion, the South Carolina partisan leader of the Revolutionary War. Only the title page and detailed contents are present here, tracing Marion youth, a shipwreck, Cherokee campaign service, Fort Moultrie, and the making of Marion Brigade. Later chapters promise Tory surprises at Nelson Ferry and Black Mingo and a pursuit by Tarleton. The biography itself, by the author of a history of South Carolina, is not included in this record.
the-life-of-general-francis-marion: Mason Locke Weems wrote his popular life of General Francis Marion, the Swamp Fox of the Revolutionary War. Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here, giving the book title, Weems name, and a March 1997 electronic release note. The header also explains that the text was transcribed twice and compared by machine to catch errors. The biography itself, with Marion partisan raids in South Carolina, stays beyond the pages held in this record at all.
the-life-of-horatio-lord-nelson:
Robert Southey wrote his life of Horatio Nelson as a clear, short manual a young sailor could carry and learn by heart. His opening chapter covers 1758 to 1783. Nelson was born on September 29, 1758, at Burnham Thorpe parsonage in Norfolk, where his father Edmund was rector.

Southey lists boyhood service in the Raisonnable, a merchant voyage to the West Indies, Arctic sailing with Captain Phipps, and East Indies duty in ill health. Promotion followed through the American war years. Southey treats a faithful record of Nelson actions as the best praise any writer could offer.
the-life-of-lord-byron:
A life of Lord Byron opens with family history reaching back to William the Conqueror. No author is named on these opening pages. Companions of the Conqueror named Erneis and Ralph head the line, under early spellings Buron and Biron.

Ralph, the poet direct ancestor, held Crown lands in Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire and lived at Horestan Castle. Later Byrons gained the manor of Rochdale under Edward I and fought under Henry V. One joined Henry VII at Bosworth and became constable of Nottingham Castle. Pedigree fills the first chapter before Byron troubled childhood and title appear.
the-life-of-sir-richard-burton:
Thomas Wright wrote his life of Sir Richard Burton fifteen years after Burton death. His preface treats Lady Burton earlier biography with pity and sharp blame. She wrote while dying of an incurable disease, racing to praise her husband and answer his enemies.

Her book, Wright says, amounts to a huge scrapbook of cuttings with no original anecdote and only her own view of Burton. He promises to fix her errors and fill her gaps. Readers get a corrective life of the explorer, linguist, and swordsman who reached Mecca and hunted the Nile sources.
the-life-of-the-venerable-mother-mary-of:
A religious of the Ursuline community wrote the life of Mother Mary of the Incarnation, founder of the Quebec Ursulines. An introduction names her chief materials. Mary son wrote a life in 1677 from her own accounts of grace and from thirty years of letters sent from Canada.

Mary wrote her inner life twice under orders from confessors, in 1633 and again in 1654. Quebec Ursuline annals add letters and Jesuit reports. Readers meet a widow who crossed the Atlantic in 1639, taught Native and French girls, and shaped early Canadian church life in lasting ways. Her letters carry much of that history firsthand.
the-long-vacation: Charlotte M. Yonge's The Long Vacation is dated 1895 in its heading. The record holds only a title page and contents, leaving the novel itself unread, though the contents promise a preface. The fourteen chapter titles shown include A Chapter of Retrospect, Darby and Joan, Slum, Sea, or Season, St. Andrew's Rock, The Hope of Vanderkist, The Mouse-Trap, Noblesse Oblige, and Heroes and Hero-Worship. A companion record of the same book does carry the preface text, while this one stops at the contents list.
the-mansion:
Henry van Dyke's The Mansion opens on the Weightman mansion, a house of calm and reserved opulence on an avenue no longer fashionable for residence. Its chocolate-colored stone front, heavy cornices, and broad plate-glass windows are not beautiful, van Dyke says, but eminently respectable and imposing. The house seems half-disdainful of the jewelers, milliners, and florists crowding its neighborhood, since its foundations lie in high finance.

John Weightman is like the house he built himself into thirty years ago: solid, correct, and justly successful, a self-made man who followed an esteemed pattern. Inside are a Louis Quinze reception-room, an Empire drawing-room, and a Jacobean dining-room, with Barbizon pictures, Barye bronzes, Rodin marbles, Persian carpets, and Chinese porcelains, all carefully kept up to date. Van Dyke builds his tale on a rich man's house as the portrait of his soul.
the-marrow-of-tradition: Charles W. Chesnutt published The Marrow of Tradition in 1901, a novel of the American South. Only the contents page and a short verse epigraph are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The thirty-seven chapter titles name a christening party, a cakewalk, and a shocking crime. Later titles cover a lynching, missing papers, and a gathering storm, then close with 'Fiat Justitia' and 'The Sisters.' Even in outline, the contents trace Southern families moving toward violence.
the-merry-devil-of-edmonton:
The Merry Devil of Edmonton is an old English comedy built around Peter Fabell, a scholar remembered for magic and merry tricks. Its cast list mixes three knightly families, the Clares, Mounchenseys, and Jerninghams, with local figures such as Banks the miller of Waltham and Smug the smith of Edmonton. Fabel himself appears in the cast as the Merry Devil, alongside a spirit named Coreb. The prologue speaks first, asking the audience for silence and attention.

The prologue explains that Fabell's fame has been forgotten by writers of the latter age. It places his birth and home in Middlesex, not fully seven miles from London. For his sleights and magic he was called the merry friend of Edmonton, the prologue says, mangling the town's name in the old spelling. Readers meet a folk magician of local legend stepping onto the stage as both scholar and devil.
the-mirrors-of-washington:
Biographical notes arranged as contents are all that is present here for The Mirrors of Washington, so none of its portrait essays appear. The notes give compact career summaries for the public men the volume treats. Warren G. Harding heads the list, with his Ohio newspaper years, senate service, and presidency beginning in 1921.

Woodrow Wilson's note runs longer, tracing Davidson and Princeton, a law degree, the Princeton presidency, and the New Jersey governorship. His two presidential terms and his 1918 sailing for France at the head of the peace commission are recorded. George Brinton McClellan Harvey follows, with his newspaper career, his purchase of the North American Review in 1899, and his years as president of Harper and Brothers.
the-mission:
Captain Marryat's The Mission, or Scenes in Africa, was written for young people. George Routledge and Sons published it in London and New York. Only its title page and contents are present here, so no chapter text appears. Marryat's other tales, from Frank Mildmay and Jacob Faithful to Phantom Ship, are listed on the title page.

The contents summarise the opening chapters in detail. Sir Charles Wilmot has lost the ship Grosvenor and doubts whether his wife and children survived the wreck. His kinsman Alexander Wilmot forms a plan, wins reluctant consent, and sails for the Cape. Fellow passengers, talk of natural history, and accounts of Dutch treatment of the Hottentots fill the early chapter headings.
the-moon:
Thomas Gwyn Elger's The Moon, published in London and Liverpool in 1895, is present here only in title page and contents, so its description of lunar features does not appear. Elger directed the Lunar Section of the British Astronomical Association and had presided over the Liverpool Astronomical Society. The subtitle promises a full description and map of the moon's principal physical features.

Contents show the plan: a history of selenography, the study of the moon's surface, and lunar photography, then a catalogue of formations. The catalogue marches quadrant by quadrant in twenty-degree bands of longitude, west and east. An Italian epigraph from Ariosto's Orlando Furioso heads the title page.
the-mysterious-island-the-secret-of-the-:
The Secret of the Island, translated by W. H. G. Kingston from Jules Verne, forms the third part, completing The Mysterious Island. An introduction explains that the tales ran in a famous Paris magazine for younger readers as part of Verne's Voyages Extraordinaires. Printed in Everyman's Library in 1909 by arrangement with Sampson Low, Marston and Company, the volume is ranked by its introducer next to Robinson Crusoe among island tales.

Kingston, the introduction notes, died before this printing, and his name also appears on the title as translator. A long list of Verne's works in English follows, with translators and dates. Five Weeks in a Balloon and A Journey to the Centre of the Earth appear there. Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea is listed too, and several entries are in Kingston's own versions.
the-native-son:
Inez Haynes Irwin's The Native Son opens with an elaborate dedication to men who, in her phrase, translated California to her. James W. Coffroth, Meyer Cohn, Porter Garnett, and others are listed as proud native sons. A longer roll of apologetic adopted sons follows, including Gelett Burgess and Fremont Older; Perry Newberry's name appears twice in that second list, a plain duplication in the printing.

The book itself begins wryly. The only drawback to writing about California, Irwin says, is that scenery, climate, and even weather will creep in. Anything produced ends up sounding halfway between a railroad folder, meaning a railway publicity pamphlet, and a circus advertisement, whatever the writer intends.
the-new-physics-and-its-evolution:
Lucien Poincare's The New Physics and Its Evolution was published in New York by D. Appleton and Company in 1909 as the authorised translation of his French work La Physique Moderne. Poincare served as one of France's nineteen inspectors-general of public instruction, visiting universities and lycees and reporting on their studies. A prefatory note, written for this translation, introduces him to English readers.

That position, the note argues, let him value the revolution in physical science while staying clear of the quarrels over radium and the constitution of matter. The translator, who does not sign a name in these pages, confesses that packing a decade of discovery into some 300 pages made the book dense for untrained readers. An extended contents digest and full indexes were added to help.
the-new-south-a-chronicle-of-social-and-:
Holland Thompson's The New South, dated 1919 and subtitled A Chronicle of Social and Industrial Evolution, surveys the region in nine chapters listed in its contents. The Background and The Confederate Soldier Takes Charge open the book. The Revolt of the Common Man, The Farmer and the Land, and Industrial Development follow, with labour conditions, the problem of Black and white, and educational progress before The South of Today.

Chapter I begins with a caution. Today's South, Thompson writes, differs from the South of 1860, and even from that of 1865. A New South exists, though perhaps not with the meaning usually attached to the phrase, which has been misused in superficial discussion more often than any other expression. A chapter on the repudiation of state debts and a bibliographical note follow the main text.
the-pastor-s-son:
William W. Walter wrote The Pastor's Son and dedicated it to F. S. B. In his preface Walter says his sole reason for publishing is to call attention to another book, one holding the Christ truth that frees readers from trouble. It shows the way out of sin, heals the sick, mends grief, and gives plenty to the poor.

Walter speaks from experience. Sick for more than seven years, at the edge of the grave and reduced to poverty, he was rescued, restored to health, and made joyful. The contents list chapters from Thanksgiving Morning and What Walter Found to a first, second, and third lesson, in the Christian Science line his preface declares.
the-phantom-of-the-opera-centennial-edit: A centennial edition of Gaston Leroux's The Phantom of the Opera, listed with a 1909 date, is represented here by its table of contents alone, so the novel itself does not appear. The list names title and copyright pages and an introduction, then chapters in capital letters. Is It the Ghost?, The New Margarita, and Box Five open the tale. One title is misprinted as The Encfianted Violin. The list reaches chapter nineteen, The Viscount and the Persian, further than two sister records but short of the fullest one.
the-pivot-of-civilization:
Margaret Sanger's The Pivot of Civilization argues the case for birth control, with an introduction by H. G. Wells. Sanger dedicates the volume to Alice Drysdale Vickery. She praises Vickery's prophetic vision of liberated womanhood. A long quotation from Havelock Ellis stands at the front. It dreams of a world where women's modesty has become courage.

Chapter headings show the line of argument. They name a new truth, conscripted motherhood, the fertility of the feeble-minded, and the cruelty of charity. Later chapters name the dangers of cradle competition, science as an ally, and woman and the future. An appendix prints the principles and aims of the American Birth Control League. Wells, opening his introduction, grants that birth control is a question of fundamental importance. He still questions whether pivot is the right metaphor for it.
the-planet-mars-and-its-inhabitants-a-ps: The Planet Mars and Its Inhabitants is credited to Eros Urides, presented as a Martian of the City of Urid. Here only the front matter and contents appear, so the chapters themselves are absent. A caption explains a map of one Martian hemisphere. Side canals join larger waterways, and round spots mark reservoirs for the long summer. Most canals run double, about seventy-five miles apart. Contents entries promise the author's self-introduction, population centres and climate, the canal system, and a planetary economy where the commonwealth supplies all wants.
the-plays-of-w-e-henley-and-r-l-stevenso: The Plays of W. E. Henley and R. L. Stevenson was published by William Heinemann at London in 1907. Here only the title page, contents, and start of a cast list appear, so the plays themselves are absent. The contents give Deacon Brodie at page 1, Beau Austin at 111, Admiral Guinea at 177, and Robert Macaire at 251. Deacon Brodie, or The Double Life, is billed as a melodrama in five acts and eight tableaux. Its first person named is William Brodie, deacon of the Wrights and housebreaker.
the-poems-of-william-watson: The Poems of William Watson was published by Macmillan and Co. at New York and London in 1893. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the poems are absent. A miscellaneous section lists Prelude, Autumn, World-Strangeness, and The Mock Self. It also lists In Laleham Churchyard, The Flight of Youth, and A Child's Hair. Political pieces stand among them. They include To Lord Tennyson, a sketch of a political character, and England to Ireland. England and Her Colonies, The Russ at Kara, and Liberty Rejected appear as well.
the-poetical-works-of-mrs-leprohon:
The Poetical Works of Mrs. Leprohon, who wrote as Miss R. E. Mullins, opens with an introduction about the early literature of Canada. When the country's literature comes to be written in after ages, the writer hopes, room will be kept for the pioneers. Those pioneers gave the people of their best. They sang songs of duty, patriotism, and hope while life in the young land was still a struggle.

Mrs. Leprohon is granted a distinguished place in that band. None of the pioneers, the introduction says, put gifts of mind and heart to finer use. None ranged wider in sympathy. None served good causes with purer motives. She won the admiration and friendship of a large circle across every creed and race among her compatriots. The volume presents itself as a record of her at her best.
the-poetry-of-architecture-or-the-archit: John Ruskin's The Poetry of Architecture heads Volume I of his Complete Works in the Library Edition, sharing it with Seven Lamps of Architecture. Its subtitle promises the architecture of the nations of Europe, considered with natural scenery and national character. Here only the title pages and the start of the contents appear, so the essays themselves are absent. The contents list an introduction, then Part I on the cottage. That part begins with the lowland cottage in England and France, then in Italy.
the-power-of-concentration: Theron Q. Dumont's The Power of Concentration reaches this record through an old Project Gutenberg header, numbered Etext 1570 and dated December 1998. Only that header is present here, so the lessons themselves do not appear. It names Dumont as author and notes the text was scanned by Charles Keller with OmniPage Professional OCR software, before the usual Gutenberg notices. No title page, contents, or chapter text can be seen in what is present.
the-principles-of-masonic-law-a-treatise: Albert G. Mackey's Principles of Masonic Law, a treatise on the constitutional laws, usages, and landmarks of Freemasonry, was published in New York in 1856. Mackey signs himself Grand Lecturer and Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of South Carolina. A Cicero motto heads the title page. The book is dedicated to Brother J. J. J. Gourgas as a testimonial of friendship and veneration. The pages at hand end within that dedication; the treatise itself is not reached.
the-profits-of-religion-an-essay-in-econ: Upton Sinclair's The Profits of Religion, second in a series by him, is identified in its Project Gutenberg header as Etext 1558, dated December 1998 and last updated in March 2003. The pages provided hold that old-style header alone, with its copyright cautions and notes on how Gutenberg texts are prepared. Sinclair's essay itself, subtitled an essay in economic interpretation, does not appear in the pages at hand.
the-profits-of-religion-fifth-edition: Upton Sinclair's The Profits of Religion appears here in its fifth edition, printed by Vanguard Press, with printings listed from January 1927. In his Offertory, Sinclair calls the book a study of supernaturalism as income for some and protection for privilege, the work of twenty-five years of thought. A note dated 1926 says the text is unchanged since 1917 and records over 60,000 copies sold. The pages at hand hold these preliminaries only, not the essay's chapters.
the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-d-d-vo:
Volume IX of Swift's Prose Works gathers his contributions to The Tatler, The Examiner, The Spectator, and The Intelligencer. Temple Scott edited the volume, published by George Bell in 1902 with a portrait after Charles Jervas. The editorial essay shown describes Swift's Examiner work as a new kind of examining, unaccustomed to Whigs and Tories alike. The paper was welcomed across the kingdom and did the ministry's intended work magnificently, though not lastingly.

Swift laid on Harley and St. John a burden heavier than they could carry, the essay argues, and they fell when his support ended. His genius shows a rare combination of qualities, and his personality stands out above his work. His lot, the essay says, was always to serve rather than to command, a servitude accepted with the priest's robe. Dr. Johnson's admission about Swift is noted as deserving repeated record.
the-psychology-of-revolution: Gustave Le Bon's The Psychology of Revolution opens with a full contents list. An introduction promises a fresh reading of history, and Part I studies what drives revolts. Book I sorts revolts into kinds, then turns to revolts of faith, from the Reformation's first days to clashes between creeds. A third chapter weighs why rulers resist so weakly. The pages provided hold the scan note and this list alone; Le Bon's text itself is not shown.
the-rayner-slade-amalgamation: J. S. Fletcher lays out a mystery in chapters dated 1922, beginning with a midnight ride and a dead man, then a shoe buckle and the introduction of Mr. Franklin Fullaway. Headings promise stolen jewels tied to a prima donna's portrait, a frantic impresario, a jewel box, and a second and third murder as suspicion hardens. Here only the title and chapter list are present, so the investigation itself does not appear.
the-recitation:
George Herbert Betts taught psychology at Cornell College in Iowa. He treats classroom recitation in a Riverside Educational Monograph. Henry Suzzallo edited the series. Houghton Mifflin issued the book with copyrights of 1910 and 1911. Five chapters cover the work. They treat purposes, method, and the art of questioning. They also treat good conditions and the assignment of lessons.

Betts divides teaching into two great functions. One function organizes and manages the school. The other does the actual teaching. Teachers today meet an early attempt at studied questioning here. Questioning becomes a skill, not a habit. The plain structure still suits beginners. It shows how lessons are led, step by step.
the-recreations-of-a-country-parson:
A. K. H. Boyd offers a second series of essays from Boston in 1862. Each chapter concerns some part of a clergyman's life. Topics run from choosing town or country to disappointment and success. Churchyards, summer days, and solitary days follow. The Scottish pulpit gets a chapter of its own. The first essay counts one happy circumstance in a clergyman's lot. He is spared painful doubt about where to spend his days.

Boyd writes with gentle irony throughout. He pities even a man returning rich from Australia. Such a man has no calling to guide his money. Later chapters visit Glasgow and a water-cure. Friends meet in council before the conclusion. Readers get Victorian clerical life in reflective prose. The tone stays companionable from start to finish.
the-red-horizon: Patrick MacGill's war book appeared at Toronto and at London in 1916. Viscount Esher supplied a foreword. The title pages list MacGill's earlier books. They cover navvy life and a rat-pit. They also cover an amateur army and a great push. Only the title pages are present here. Publisher's lists and a note on corrected errors appear with them. The front-line narrative itself does not appear on these pages.
the-redemption-of-david-corson: Charles Frederic Goss published his religious novel in 1900. The Bowen-Merrill Company issued it. He dedicated it to William Harvey Anderson. Thirty-five chapters trace a fall and a recovery. Biblical language shapes their titles throughout. Another Eden opens the tale, and Satan arrives. Egyptians, a woman, and a light that lies follow. A serpent's trail leads toward broken reeds. Poisoned springs mark the depths of the fall. Only the title pages and dedication are present here. The full chapter list appears with them. The redemption itself does not appear.
the-religious-situation:
Goldwin Smith asks what the world would be without religion, in an essay issued at Toronto in 1908 after appearing in the North American Review. He opens with Bishop Butler's caution that reason is the only faculty we have to judge anything, even revelation itself.

Smith wonders whether the social fabric could stand if belief in a divine dispensation, with compensation hereafter for inequality here, were lost. The question, he says, now presents itself everywhere. Readers meet a liberal Victorian thinker weighing faith's social uses at a moment of doubt, in prose that is anxious rather than triumphant.
the-reminiscences-of-sir-henry-hawkins-b:
Sir Henry Hawkins, Baron Brampton, opens his reminiscences with a preface dated at Harrogate on August 17, 1904, saying pressure alone persuaded him to publish. He credits the whole merit of the volume to his old friend Richard Harris, who edited it.

Harris shaped innumerable manuscript notes and long conversations into readable form, as he had earlier done for Hawkins's part in the Tichborne case. Hawkins thanks him warmly and calls his own contributions imperfect. Readers of legal memoir get a famous judge presented through an editor he plainly trusted, with courtroom reputation doing much of the work.
the-rifle-and-the-hound-in-ceylon:
Sir Samuel White Baker writes a new preface more than twenty years after his Ceylon hunting book first appeared, noting nine later years of African exploration. Breech-loading rifles have replaced muzzle-loaders, he says, giving hunters of dangerous game an added safeguard.

Baker also defends the heavy powder charges he used thirty years earlier and that critics once called absurd, now accepted as the route to velocity, low trajectory, range, penetration, and precision. Few men had handled a rifle when he began thirty-seven years before. Sporting readers get memoir, natural history, and firearms debate in one voice.
the-roman-question: E. About's study, translated from the French by H. C. Coape and issued by Appleton at New York in 1859, asks how the pope rules as a king. Contents move through the necessity and patrimony of temporal power, its subjects by class from plebeians to nobility, foreigners, the absolute character of that power, Pius the Ninth, and Cardinal Antonelli. Here only the title pages and opening of the contents list are present, so the argument itself does not appear.
the-romance-of-isabel-lady-burton: Isabel Burton's life story, told partly by herself and partly by W. H. Wilkins, reaches a second volume in a third edition issued by Hutchinson at London in 1897 with portraits and illustrations. Contents for the volume begin with book two continued at chapter eleven. Here only the title pages and opening of the contents list are present, so Lady Burton's narrative itself does not appear.
the-romantic-settlement-of-lord-selkirk-: Dr. George Bryce of Winnipeg wrote The Romantic Settlement of Lord Selkirk's Colonists. Its subtitle is The Pioneers of Manitoba. The Musson Book Company of Toronto copyrighted it in 1909. A frontispiece shows Thomas, fifth Earl of Selkirk. He founded the Red River Colony in 1812. Only the opening pages and the start of the contents are present. Bryce's narrative itself does not appear. The first chapter is called Patriarch's Story. Its sections treat an extinct race and earlier peoples. Others cover Montreal merchants and the dusky riders of the plain.
the-rover-boys-in-business-or-the-search:
The Search for the Missing Bonds subtitles the nineteenth Rover Boys volume, dated 1915. Arthur M. Winfield wrote the book, and its introduction recaps the earlier volumes. They run from At School through In Alaska, where the lads were last met.

Readers learn that Dick is now married. He runs his father's business in New York City and elsewhere. Tom and Sam are at Brill College. After a great baseball game, the younger brothers get a startling message from Dick. He summons them to New York at once. Bonds of great value have mysteriously disappeared. Unless they are recovered, the Rover fortune may be seriously impaired.
the-satyricon-volume-01-introduction:
Volume one of the Satyricon of Petronius Arbiter serves as the introduction to W. C. Firebaugh's complete and unexpurgated translation. That translation incorporates the forgeries of Nodot and Marchena. It also uses readings introduced by De Salas. The same title block heads the later volumes of this set.

Firebaugh's essay reflects on the translator's difficulties. A conscientious translator feels his own unworthiness first, he says. Allusions familiar to the author may baffle later generations. He praises older versions, such as Melmouth's Pliny and Adlington's Golden Ass. Languages change, and slang changes fastest, he argues. A rendering in the slang of 1898 already sounds dated. No rendering of Petronius's street speech can ever be final, in his view.
the-second-funeral-of-napoleon:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote The Second Funeral of Napoleon under the name Michael Angelo Titmarsh. The piece falls into three parts. They treat the disinterment of Napoleon at St. Helena, the voyage to Paris, and the funeral ceremony. It is framed as a letter to a dear correspondent.

Thackeray begins with a difficulty in telling greatness from meanness. Reading history has often puzzled him, he confesses. He cannot always tell whether to laud a character or fling the book aside. He teases his correspondent, Miss Smith, about her school histories. Goldsmith, Hume, and Smollett are named. Their other works, he jokes, are the true pictures of human life. The Vicar of Wakefield is one, he says. Modern historians know very little, he warns. They tell only a little of what they know.
the-second-generation:
David Graham Phillips published The Second Generation in 1906. He also wrote The Cost and The Plum Tree, the title page notes. Twenty-eight chapters are listed in the contents. Early titles command, Put your house in order. Of somebodies and nobodies, Mrs. Whitney intervenes, and the shattered colossus follow. A will and a jilting come after.

Later headings bring Arthur among lawyers, then rescued. Madelene and Lorry's romance appear, along with Hiram's son. Charles Whitney's heirs and the dead that live close the list. Chapter one opens just before a noon whistle. In six minutes it would blow, the text begins. The workmen are introduced, and the account breaks off there in the portion shown.
the-second-honeymoon: Ruby M. Ayres wrote The Second Honeymoon, copyrighted in 1921 by W. J. Watt and Company. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York. Ayres also wrote A Bachelor Husband and The Scar, the title page says. The pages shown give the title matter and contents only. The text stops at the heading of chapter one. Twenty-three chapters trace Jimmy and Christine. Early titles promise the past intervening and a jilting. Sangster takes a hand and speaks in riddles later. Bitterness, too late, and the unexpected close the list.
the-shadow-line-a-confession:
Joseph Conrad subtitled The Shadow-Line a confession. He dedicated it to Borys and to all others who crossed, in early youth, the shadow-line of their generation with love. An epigraph from Baudelaire heads part one. The first chapter opens with a claim about youth. Only the young have such moments, Conrad writes.

He does not mean the very young, he clarifies. Early youth lives in advance of its days, in a continuity of hope. One closes the little gate of mere boyishness behind one, he says. An enchanted garden follows, its shades glowing with promise. In time a shadow-line appears ahead, warning that early youth must be left behind. The moments he means are those of boredom, weariness, and dissatisfaction, he explains.
the-sheriff-s-son: William MacLeod Raine wrote The Sheriff's Son, published by Grosset and Dunlap in April 1918. Harold Cue illustrated it. Raine dedicated the book to Robert H. Davis. With his usual generosity to writers, he gave the author the germ idea of the plot as a present, the dedication says. The pages shown give the title and dedication matter. The contents portion lists a single heading, chapter twenty-nine, A New Leaf. No chapter text follows, so the western story itself cannot be described from what is preserved here.
the-sign-of-the-red-cross-a-tale-of-old-:
Evelyn Everett-Green subtitled The Sign of the Red Cross a tale of old London. Chapter one is called A Warning Whisper. The Master Builder cries that he does not believe a word of it, to open the scene. Such scares are just old stories, he insists. Some poor wretch dies of sweating sickness or spotted fever, he says. At once all mouths are full of the plague.

Rachel Harmer answers beside her spinning wheel. Heaven send he may be right, she says. Yet the vice of the city and the wickedness of the Court might draw down God's judgments, she warns. The Master Builder, Charles Mason, shifts uneasily. Times are good for him, the narrator explains. Fine ladies send for him to alter houses, and money flows into his pocket. His wife goes about fine, and his idle son leads a notorious band of Scourers.
the-sins-of-severac-bablon: Sax Rohmer's The Sins of Severac Bablon is dated 1914 in its header. The copy shown was formatted in 2007 by Munsey's. Its pages give a chapter list of nineteen titles and no story text. Mr. Julius Rohscheimer is introduced first. Thirty men who were all alike and the head of Cesar follow. A mystic hand and the shadow of Severac Bablon come next. Es-Sindibad of Cadogan Gardens appears at chapter nine. The lamp and the mask and the Damascus curtain are promised later. Three letters close the list shown.
the-sketch-book-of-geoffrey-crayon: Washington Irving's 1819 masterpiece: "Rip Van Winkle," "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow," and sketches of England and America. The book that made American literature respectable abroad. Charming, graceful, and immortal. Irving's gentle humor made him the first American author famous in Europe.
the-small-house-at-allington:
Anthony Trollope's The Small House at Allington comes with an editorial note on its first publication. It ran serially in the Cornhill Magazine from September 1862 to April 1864.
