Smith, Elder issued it in book form in 1864. John Everett Millais supplied eighteen full-page illustrations, the note says. Quarter-page vignettes by Millais opened nineteen chapters in the serial.

The contents place the squire of Allington first. The two pearls of Allington and the widow Dale follow. Mrs. Roper's boarding-house and beautiful days come next. The beginning of troubles arrives at chapter seven. Lilian Dale becomes a butterfly at chapter twelve. John Eames takes a walk, and Mr. Crosbie meets an old clergyman, in the portion of the list shown.
the-soul-of-the-indian-an-interpretation: Charles Alexander Eastman, who also bore the name Ohiyesa, wrote this interpretation of Native American spiritual life. He dedicates it to his wife, Elaine Goodale Eastman, thanking her for companionship in thought and work. The opening pages present here carry that dedication and verses by Sidney Lanier, Thomas Campbell, and Coleridge on nature and God. They close at the heading of a foreword, so the foreword's own words and the chapters themselves do not appear.
the-spenders-a-tale-of-the-third-generat: Harry Leon Wilson published this novel in 1902, subtitled a tale of the third generation and illustrated by O'Neill Latham. The pages present here give the title page and contents only. Twelve chapters show the second generation removed and Billy Brue finding his man. The West clashes with the East, and Uncle Peter Bines cuts loose, so the story itself does not appear.
the-story-of-evolution:
Joseph McCabe published this account of evolution in 1912. His preface opens with a fancy. A traveller moves into space faster than light. He could overtake the light that once fell on past events. The French Revolution and the Reformation would pass before him. The ancient empires would follow. He would read human history in reverse. McCabe says something like that panorama has truly become possible, not through light but through records in soil and rock.

Modern science, he argues, has deciphered those records into an outline picture of the growth of heavens and earth, with details left to future generations. His volume aims to give that story in clear, plain language. It gathers new findings from a score of sciences. It covers suns and atoms. Hills and elephants, fishes and flowers follow. Man and his institutions close the survey.
the-story-of-the-american-legion-the-bir: George Seay Wheat tells the birth of the American Legion in the first of a planned series issued after each annual national convention, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons of New York and London in 1919. Only the title pages and contents are present in this record, listing chapters on latter war days in France, the Paris caucus of March 1919, the advance committee, the St. Louis caucus of May 1919, the Legion and the Bolsheviki, and the re-employment problem, so Wheat's narrative itself does not appear.
the-strange-visitation:
Marie Corelli opens this tale on a wild night of storm and quarrel. She also wrote The Sorrows of Satan and Thelma. A gale scratches and howls at the doors and windows. It sounds like an angry cat. Cold rain sweeps down on the shrieking blast. Yet this night of all nights calls for peace and goodwill, she observes. Those are the season's proper influences. It is Christmas Eve.

Corelli pauses the story to meditate on that anniversary. She recalls the host of angels. They sang a hymn of pardon to mankind on that first Christmas Eve. She quotes Milton's lines too. In them no war or battle's sound was heard. Kings sat still, knowing their sovereign Lord was by.
the-suppressed-poems-of-alfred-lord-tenn: J. C. Thomson edited this collection of Tennyson's suppressed poems from 1830 to 1868. Only the title page and the opening of a contents list appear in this record. The prize poem Timbuctoo leads off. The Poems Chiefly Lyrical group follows. Its pieces include The Burial of Love and Hero to Leander. The Mystic and The Grasshopper appear too. Several sonnets and songs come next. Contributions to periodicals from 1831 and 1832 close the heads. The poems themselves do not appear.
the-tale-of-fatty-coon: Arthur Scott Bailey's Sleepy-Time tale of Fatty Coon was published by Grosset and Dunlap under a 1915 copyright, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. Only the title page and a contents list are present in this record, showing thirteen chapters in which Fatty is at home, learns something about eggs, discovers Mrs. Turtle's secret, goes fishing, meets the green corn and a monster, and hears Jasper Jay's news, so Fatty's own adventures do not appear.
the-tower-of-london:
W. Harrison Ainsworth's Tower of London, first published serially in 1840, is presented here by the 1873 Press with a publisher's essay celebrating historical fiction's golden age. Ainsworth, the editors note, was among the most popular Victorian novelists, author of thirty-nine novels and owner of journals including Bentley's Miscellany. His Rookwood made Dick Turpin famous and launched Ainsworth into London's highest literary circles, where Dickens and Thackeray were his friends.

The novel itself, set in 1553 and 1554, follows Lady Jane Grey's doomed bid for the crown and her execution, with Northumberland's fall and Wyatt's rising around it. Queen Mary, Princess Elizabeth, Cranmer, and Gardiner all appear. The publishers praise Ainsworth's gothic manner, broad comedy, and carefully researched Old London, promising pageantry anchored in the Tower's stones.
the-tragedy-of-pudd-nhead-wilson: Mark Twain's Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson was published at Hartford by the American Publishing Company in 1894, copyrighted by Olivia L. Clemens. This record gives the title page and a full contents list, stopping where Twain's 'Whisper to the Reader' begins. The chapters promise Roxy's shrewd trick, the changelings' ways, the twins thrilling Dawson's Landing, Pudd'nhead's startling discovery, and a doom-laden close. Twain's murder mystery of switched babies and fingerprint evidence is fully outlined here, while his prose waits beyond the contents page.
the-trimmed-lamp-and-other-stories-of-th: O. Henry's Trimmed Lamp and Other Stories of the Four Million is laid out here in a frontispiece, title page, and contents list, with the title story breaking off after its first sentence. The contents name twenty-five New York tales, among them Two Thanksgiving Day Gentlemen, The Last Leaf, A Harlem Tragedy, and The Purple Dress. The frontispiece shows a suitor wooing a shopgirl across her counter, grand as King Cophetua. O. Henry's shopgirls and clerks are announced, though their stories wait past the opening line given.
the-triumph-of-john-kars-a-story-of-the-: Ridgwell Cullum's Triumph of John Kars is a story of the Yukon, copyrighted in 1917. It is present here as title page and contents. A coloured frontispiece carries a caption reporting the defenders reduced to four. Sixteen chapters run from Fort Mowbray and the Mission of St. Agatha through Bell River, Snake River Landing, the man with the scar, and the secret of the gorge. Cullum's northern adventure is outlined in these headings, while John Kars himself waits beyond them.
the-two-wives-or-lost-and-won:
T. S. Arthur published his household tale in Philadelphia in 1851, as the third volume in Arthur's Library for the Household. A short preface states the design plainly. Tender, self-forgetting love can win a straying husband back from the edge of ruin, while a wife lacking those virtues brings sad results under similar trials.

Chapter one opens at evening in the Wilkinsons' neat room, where a shaded lamp burns and a wife watches her husband rise restlessly from his book. She begs him not to go out, since evenings are their only shared hours. That small domestic tension carries the moral contrast the preface announces between a marriage lost and a marriage won.
the-tysons-mr-and-mrs-nevill-tyson: May Sinclair, already known for The Divine Fire and The Helpmate, published The Tysons in 1906. Only the title page and contents list are present in this record, so the novel's chapters do not appear. Sixteen chapters are named, moving from separate introductions of Mr. Nevill Tyson and his wife to their life at home. Later headings promise a first stone, a night watch, a son and heir, and a chapter called An Unnatural Mother. Circumstantial evidence, a return likened to Odysseus, a fire, and a new life close the list.
the-unbearable-bassington:
H. H. Munro, writing as Saki, published The Unbearable Bassington with John Lane in London and New York. The copy shown here is a sixth edition dated 1913 in Roman numerals. His author's note is brief and dry: the story has no moral, and where it points out an evil it offers no remedy.

Chapter one seats Francesca Bassington in her Blue Street drawing-room, taking China tea and cress sandwiches with her brother Henry. The meal is described with elegant precision, poised between luncheon and dinner. Readers meet a polished London household rendered in Saki's cool, amused prose, with social comedy carrying the scene rather than any stated lesson.
the-underdogs-a-novel-of-the-mexican-rev:
Mariano Azuela wrote The Underdogs, the novel of the Mexican Revolution, after serving that struggle at first hand. Born in Lagos de Moreno in 1873, he trained as a doctor in Guadalajara and backed Madero's uprising against the Díaz dictatorship. After Madero's assassination he joined Pancho Villa's army as a physician.

Driven into exile at El Paso, he wrote Los de abajo there in 1915, drawing on knowledge gained in the field. General recognition waited until 1924, when critics hailed the story as the novel of the Revolution. The introductory account also traces his later disillusion, as self-servers turned hopes for Mexico's poor into their own ladder.
the-united-states-constitution:
An early Project Gutenberg edition presents the Constitution of the United States of America from 1787. Its editors explain that the text keeps variant spellings, punctuation, and capitalization believed to belong to the original. They also note plainly that amendments are excluded here, since the Bill of Rights was issued separately.

The document opens with the famous preamble about forming a more perfect Union and securing the blessings of liberty. Article one then vests all legislative powers in a Congress of Senate and House. Section two sets House members' terms at two years and requires representatives to be twenty-five years old, seven years a citizen, and residents of their state when elected.
the-united-states-in-the-light-of-prophe:
Uriah Smith published The United States in the Light of Prophecy in 1874, built as an exposition of Revelation chapter thirteen, verses eleven to seventeen. His preface argues that prophetic light now converges on the present age. Events soon to come, he says, make any apology for the treatise unnecessary.

Smith asks what part the United States must play in the scenes prophecy describes. A nation risen so suddenly to greatness, he reasons, must be a subject of divine prophecy or at least providence. The pages ahead promise a brief but scriptural answer. He admits the treatment is not exhaustive, yet hopes his case will stir readers to further inquiry.
the-unity-of-western-civilization: F. S. Marvin arranged and edited The Unity of Western Civilization, published by Oxford University Press in 1915. The record here presents the title page and contents, so the essays themselves do not appear. Marvin contributes an introduction on the grounds of unity, and J. L. Myres writes on prehistoric times. J. A. Smith covers Greece and Rome, Ernest Barker the Middle Ages, and W. M. Geldart law. Later essays treat European literature and art, science and philosophy as unifying forces, western education, and commerce and finance.
the-use-and-need-of-the-life-of-carry-a-: Carry A. Nation is named as author of The Use and Need of the Life of Carry A. Nation. Nothing of the book itself is present in this record beyond the project header and the title and author lines, so no preface, contents, or narrative appears. Readers are given only the bare identification: a life of the temperance campaigner, written by Nation herself, arguing in its title that such a life is useful and needed. The episodes she recounts cannot be described from what is preserved here.
the-valley-of-decision:
Edith Wharton sets The Valley of Decision in Italy and dedicates the novel to Paul and Minnie Bourget, remembering Italian days together. A biblical line about multitudes in the valley of decision stands as motto. The contents divide the story into four books: The Old Order, The New Light, The Choice, and The Reward.

Book one opens in a small neglected chapel at February dusk. Farm noises drift through closed doors, and a slanting ray of sun picks out a pale haloed head on the chancel wall, the ravaged face of the saint of Assisi. Filomena scolds a little white-faced foundling in the kitchen nearby. Wharton's scene joins decay, faith, and domestic life in one quiet picture.
the-valley-of-the-moon:
Jack London opens The Valley of the Moon inside a sweltering commercial laundry. Saxon, a piece-work ironer of fancy starch work, listens to a girl urging her toward the Bricklayers' picnic at Weasel Park. Dancing, tug-of-war, fat-man races, and Irish jigging are promised for the next day.

Work dominates the scene instead. An elderly woman, worn down by age, pregnancy, and seven children, collapses at her board after dropping a hot iron on the cloth. Fellow ironers rush first to save the garment, then to help her, while a forewoman hurries down the aisle. London grounds his heroine's hopes for escape in heat, fatigue, and the money-loss tremor running through the room.
the-variation-of-animals-and-plants-unde: Charles Darwin's Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication is presented here as volumes one and two together, although separate single-volume records also exist in the library. What appears in this record is the detailed contents, so the chapters themselves do not appear. Summaries announce a foreword, a preface to the second edition, and an introduction. Chapter one treats domestic dogs and cats, covering ancient varieties, barking learned and lost, and feral animals. Chapter two moves to horses and asses, and chapter three to pigs, cattle, sheep, and goats.
the-voice-of-the-city-further-stories-of: O. Henry collects twenty-five New York stories in The Voice of the City, subtitled Further Stories of the Four Million and published in 1919. The record here presents the title page and contents, so the stories themselves do not appear. The title story leads, followed by The Complete Life of John Hopkins and A Lickpenny Lover. Middle entries include While the Auto Waits, One Thousand Dollars, and Squaring the Circle. Later titles promise Transients in Arcadia, The Rathskeller and the Rose, and The Memento.
the-war-poems-of-siegfried-sassoon:
William Heinemann published The War Poems of Siegfried Sassoon in London in 1919. A long French epigraph from Henri Barbusse's Le Feu describes exhausted survivors grasping how hideous war is, morally and physically. A short note explains the gathering: of sixty-four poems, twelve appear for the first time, and the rest were selected from two previous volumes.

The pages present here stop inside the contents list, so the poems themselves do not appear. Early titles include Prelude: The Troops, Dreamers, The Redeemer, Trench Duty, Wirers, and Break of Day. A Working Party and Stand-To: Good Friday Morning follow, with In the Pink closing the visible list. Front-line labour and dawn stand-tos plainly supply the subjects.
the-way-of-ambition: Robert Hichens, author of The Garden of Allah, published The Way of Ambition with Frederick A. Stokes in New York, copyrighted in 1913. J. H. Gardner Soper supplied a colour frontispiece and four illustrations. A frontispiece caption quotes a question about an extraordinary Cornish genius named Charmian. Two records in the library carry this same Stokes edition; this one presents the title pages and the first lines of a contents list, so the novel itself does not appear. Only the bare numbers of chapters one and two can be read.
the-works-of-rudyard-kipling-one-volume-: A one-volume edition of Rudyard Kipling's works is represented by the start of its contents list. Departmental Ditties and Other Verses form the first volume within it. Poems listed include General Summary and The Story of Uriah. Recessional and The Vampire appear under other verses. Christmas in India and Pagett, M. P. also appear. The list breaks off before the whole contents, and no poems follow in these pages.
the-world-decision: Robert Herrick's The World Decision is represented here by a contents list in three parts, without the chapters themselves. Part one follows Italy hesitating, then deciding, on the eve of war. Speakers include a politician, a poet, and the piazza. Part two turns to France, its wounds, and its faith. Part three asks what the war means to America. A choice and peace close the volume's plan.
the-world-english-bible-web-revelation:
Revelation closes the World English Bible as book sixty-six. God gave this revelation to Jesus Christ, the text says. It shows servants things that must happen soon. An angel carried it to John, God's servant. John testifies to everything he saw. Readers and hearers of the prophecy are pronounced blessed. The time, John insists, is at hand.

John greets seven assemblies in Asia. Grace comes from the God who was, is, and is to come. Jesus is called the faithful witness and firstborn of the dead. Visions of judgment and a renewed creation follow. The Bible's final book blends letter, prophecy, and worship.
the-world-english-bible-web-song-of-solo:
Book twenty-two in the World English Bible is the Song of Songs, Solomon's love poem. A beloved woman longs for her lover's kisses. His love is better than wine, she says. His name is like oil poured forth. The king has brought her into his chambers, she adds. Friends join the chorus, praising such love above wine.

The woman calls herself dark yet lovely. Sun has scorched her while she kept others' vineyards. She asks where her beloved grazes his flock at noon. Speaker labels help readers follow the lovers and friends. Desire, gardens, and seasons fill the poems. Scripture here celebrates human love without disguise.
the-world-s-best-poetry-volume-03-sorrow: Title pages for volume three of The World's Best Poetry, copyrighted in 1904, are what this record offers. Bliss Carman served as editor-in-chief of the ten-volume set. John Vance Cheney and Charles G. D. Roberts were associate editors. J. D. Morris and Company published the set in Philadelphia. Volume three is themed Sorrow and Consolation. A heading for an interpreter's essay begins, but no poems follow in these pages.
the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-03-mass: A contents list for volume three of The World's Great Sermons, compiled by Grenville Kleiser in 1908, is present here. Preachers run from Massillon to Mason, as the title promises. Jonathan Edwards contributes a sermon on spiritual light. John Wesley writes on God's love to fallen man. George Whitefield's Method of Grace also appears. The sermon texts themselves do not follow in the opening pages provided.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-02-fic: Volume two of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton in 1910, appears as a contents list of fiction summaries. Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre is included, as is Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights. Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress and Cervantes's Don Quixote appear. Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is listed too. The summaries themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-03-fic: A contents list represents volume three of The World's Greatest Books, the 1910 fiction volume edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton. Dickens dominates the list with fourteen novels, from Pickwick Papers to Great Expectations. Defoe's Robinson Crusoe and Disraeli's Sybil also appear. Daudet's Tartarin of Tarascon opens the list. The book summaries themselves are absent from the pages shown here.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-04-fic: Volume four of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, is shown by its fiction contents list alone. George Eliot contributes Adam Bede, Romola, and Silas Marner. Fielding's Tom Jones and Joseph Andrews appear. Maria Edgeworth's Castle Rackrent is listed. Fouqué's Undine also appears among the summarized novels. The summaries themselves do not follow in the pages present in this record.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-05-fic: For volume five of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, the pages present give a fiction contents list. Hawthorne's Scarlet Letter and House of the Seven Gables appear. Victor Hugo contributes Les Misérables and Notre Dame de Paris. Tom Brown's Schooldays represents Thomas Hughes. Robert Hichens's Garden of Allah is also listed. The summaries themselves are not present in the pages shown.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-06-fic: Volume six of The World's Greatest Books, a 1910 volume edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, appears here as a fiction contents list. Le Fanu's Uncle Silas and Lesage's Gil Blas lead the list. Bulwer Lytton's Last Days of Pompeii appears. Malory's Morte d'Arthur also earns a place. M. G. Lewis's Gothic novel The Monk is listed under its hero's name, Ambrosio. The summaries themselves do not appear in this record.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-07-fic: A fiction contents list is what this record holds for volume seven of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton in 1910. Richardson's Pamela and Clarissa Harlowe appear. Pushkin's Captain's Daughter and Rabelais's Gargantua are listed. Charles Reade contributes three novels, including Hard Cash. Rousseau's New Heloise also appears. The summaries themselves are absent from the pages present here.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-08-fic: Volume eight of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton in 1910, is shown through its fiction contents. Mary Shelley's Frankenstein appears in the list. Walter Scott's Rob Roy and Quentin Durward continue from an earlier volume. Swift's Gulliver's Travels and Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin are included. Sterne's Tristram Shandy also appears. The summaries themselves do not follow in the pages present.
the-writings-of-john-burroughs-volume-05:
John Burroughs names volume five of his writings Pepacton, after its first chapter. His preface explains that Pepacton was the Indian name of his native stream. He was born in its watershed and passed his youth there. His kindred sleep along its banks. Much of his nature writing, he says, was gathered from that country. The name is said to mean marriage of the waters.

That meaning suits a book uniting many currents, Burroughs adds. The stream rises in a deep mountain gorge. Wild, rugged scenery crowds its narrow valley. A pious Scottish immigrant family enters the opening chapter. Readers get nature essays rooted in one beloved Catskill landscape.
the-yellow-crayon:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens The Yellow Crayon on a late summer day. Flower perfume drifts through a half-opened window. Sunlight zigzags across the floor past a blind's chink. Bees murmur over gorgeous flower beds outside. Inside, a man sits motionless in a high-backed chair. He has sat that way for a whole day and night.

His eyes fix on vacancy, and his mouth is set hard. Food placed beside him gets eaten only mechanically. A deep line cuts his forehead. Oppenheim builds mystery from stillness rather than action. Readers wonder what blow turned this man to stone. Intrigue, his trademark, clearly waits behind the quiet room.
the-young-captives-a-story-of-judah-and-:
Erasmus W. Jones published The Young Captives, a story of Judah and Babylon, in 1907. The opening scene erupts inside a royal apartment. A mysterious voice cries out against the King of Judah. The flushed king demands the insulter be dragged before him. Guards search every corner for the unseen herald. No trace of the intruder can be found.

Revelry resumes, yet the king cannot shake the warning. Its deep tone rings in his ears despite the wine. Even in wickedness, he fears the God he insults. Jones sets biblical captivity drama in a corrupt court. Young readers get danger, prophecy, and moral contrast in ancient Judah.
theory-of-circulation-by-respiration:
Emma Willard set out her theory of circulation by respiration in an article written by request for the U.S. Journal of Homoeopathy, printed in New York in 1861. Her synopsis links animal heat, expansion in the lungs, and motion of the blood. Heat, she argues, comes from respiration there.

Willard tells Dr. Marcy that retracing her own conviction is the way to convince others. She also notes her experiments often used her own body as apparatus. Readers get a nineteenth-century woman presenting a full physiological theory, with its history, in her own voice.
thirty-years-a-slave-from-bondage-to-fre:
Louis Hughes wrote his autobiography after thirty years enslaved, showing slavery on the plantation and in the planter's home. His preface argues the dead institution still deserves study because each generation learns from earlier history. Friends urged him to tell his experiences plainly.

Chapter one begins with his birth in Virginia in 1832, near Charlottesville on the Rivanna river. Sold as a small child with his mother and brothers, he passed to Dr. Louis of Scottsville, then to a merchant. Readers get firsthand testimony about sale, family separation, and plantation life.
thoughts-on-religion: George John Romanes left Thoughts on Religion, edited after his death by Charles Gore, Bishop of Worcester. Longmans published the twelfth impression at London in 1904. A contents page divides the book into two parts. Part one treats the influence of science upon religion in two essays. Part two gives notes toward a candid examination of religion, with definitions and purpose among its early sections. The contents and editor's preface listing are what is present here, so Romanes's essays themselves do not appear.
through-palestine-with-the-twentieth-mac: A transcriber's note is the only matter included in this record, and it concerns biblical references in a book about Palestine. The note explains that some references in the original seem mistaken and were left unchanged. A table pairs each printed reference with a suggested correction. Kings, Judges, Zechariah, Psalms, Matthew, and Acts all appear among the corrections, some marked uncertain. No title page, author, or chapter follows in what is present. Its account of the machine gun squadron itself does not appear here.
tom-swift-and-his-electric-runabout-or-t: The Speediest Car on the Road is the subtitle of the Tom Swift electric runabout story by Victor Appleton, laid out in twenty-five chapter headings. Tom hopes for a prize, builds the car, is captured and rescued, and suffers crossed wires before a tryout. Bank trouble, a run on the bank, a ditch, and lost power lead toward the big race and winning the prize. Chapter one is announced but no text follows it. The contents list is what is present here.
trimorphic-protennoia-mattison:
Divine Thought speaks in her own voice, three times over, in a Sethian hymn from Nag Hammadi. Trimorphic Protennoia, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives the triple-formed Primal Thought in English. Protennoia means first thought, the mind of the high God made sound.

She tells of three descents: as voice, as speech, and as word she comes down to wake the fallen. The hymn is dense with light, water, and names of power. Scholars count it among the key texts of the Sethian school. Mattison's version gives the hard, bright poem a clear path in English.
typhoon: Joseph Conrad's 1902 novella about Captain MacWhirr, a stolid, unimaginative seaman who steams his ship straight into a Pacific typhoon. The storm is described with terrifying power, and MacWhirr's stubborn simplicity becomes a kind of heroism. A masterpiece of sea writing and a study in character under pressure.
un-doc-1951-refugee-convention:
The Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees was adopted by a United Nations conference in 1951 and took force on 22 April 1954. Europe still held millions displaced by the Second World War. The hosted file pairs the full treaty text with a short modern background note. Later regional regimes built on the same base.

The treaty says who counts as a refugee. A refugee fears persecution for race, creed, nationality, social group, or political views. Such a person sits outside home and cannot or will not seek its shield. As written, the deal reached only events before 1951, in Europe or beyond by choice. A 1967 protocol erased those limits and made the cover worldwide.
un-doc-constitution-of-the-international:
The Constitution of the International Labour Organization sets up the world's labour body. It rests on a bold claim: lasting peace can rest only on social justice. Bad hours, low pay, and joblessness breed unrest that puts world peace at risk. The text folds in the Philadelphia goals adopted on 10 May 1944.

The charter builds a three-sided house. Each member sends two government delegates, one employer, and one worker to the yearly conference. A 56-seat governing body splits the same way: 28 states, 14 employers, 14 workers. A staff office in Geneva does the daily work. The listed aims run from capped hours and a living wage to equal pay and free unions.
un-doc-constitution-of-the-united-nation:
The Constitution of UNESCO was adopted in London on 16 November 1945. The founding states hold that wars start as ideas before they become battles. So peace must be built in the same place. Free schooling, open science, and shared culture are the tools chosen for that work.

The agency's aim is peace and safety through teamwork in learning, science, and culture. It must guard justice, law, and basic rights for all, with no bar of race, sex, tongue, or creed. A general conference of member states sets the policy. An executive board runs the gaps between sessions. A director-general and staff carry out the plans from Paris.
un-doc-convention-against-discrimination:
The Convention against Discrimination in Education was adopted by UNESCO's General Conference at Paris on 14 December 1960. Schools in many lands still sorted children by birth. The treaty names that sorting as a breach of the rights set out in the 1948 world rights text. It was UNESCO's first binding deal in the field.

Discrimination means any split in treatment by race, colour, sex, tongue, faith, views, roots, wealth, or birth. States must scrap laws and habits that sort pupils unfairly. Primary schooling must be free and a duty for all. Later schooling must open to all, with college entry by merit. Parents keep the right to pick schools and shape moral teaching.
un-doc-convention-of-the-world-meteorolo:
The Convention of the World Meteorological Organization was drawn up at Washington in 1947. Weather chiefs from many lands had met there that September. Storms and floods cross borders without pause. No state can read the skies alone, so the work had to be shared.

The pact sets up a standing weather body. Its jobs are to link station networks across the globe and speed the swap of weather news. Readings must follow one standard so all can use them. The science should serve farms, ships, and planes as well as scholars. A world congress of members rules the house. Regional groups and expert panels do the detailed work.
un-doc-geneva-convention-third-geneva-co:
The Third Geneva Convention was settled at a diplomatic conference at Geneva in 1949. Delegates met from April to August that year. The pact reworked a 1929 deal on prisoners of war. The fresh horrors of the Second World War drove the rewrite.

The text fixes who counts as a prisoner of war. Soldiers, militias with a clear sign and open arms, and some who follow the armies all qualify. Captives must be treated with humanity at all times. Killing, torture, and medical tests on them are banned. So are revenge acts against them. One shared article sets a floor of mercy for civil wars too. Neutral watchers and the Red Cross check the camps.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
The Conclusion closes the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. The manual surveyed a fresh class of wrongdoing. Laws in most lands had not caught up with the machines. This last part pulls the threads together.

Computer crime, it warns, will grow as networks spread across borders. One state cannot fight it alone. Shared meanings of the offences would help police team up, hand suspects over, and aid each other's probes. Safe havens must not be left open. At home, states should test their laws, train judges and police, and teach users sound habits. The time to act, the text ends, is now.

Regional Action is a passage in the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. It surveys what groups of states had done before the United Nations stepped in. Two bodies led the way: the OECD and the Council of Europe.

The OECD began its study in 1983 and reported in 1986. It listed acts every state should think of banning, from computer fraud to the tapping of data lines. The Council of Europe went further and widened the list. Its rule book for lawmakers, Recommendation R(89)9, came out on 13 September 1989. By 1992 the OECD had added guides on keeping systems safe.

Global action against crime is the theme of a chapter in the International Review of Criminal Policy, issues 43 and 44, a United Nations journal on crime prevention and justice. The chapter dates from the early 1990s. It starts from a simple claim: crime crosses borders faster than any one state can respond.

The text makes the case for joint moves by governments, police forces, and courts. It stresses shared plans, shared data, and help for states with fewer resources. The chapter captures a moment when crime policy was turning into a shared world task, not a purely national one.
un-doc-world-food-summit-plan-of-action:
Heads of government at the 1996 World Food Summit in Rome adopted this plan of action to cut world hunger. The summit was run by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. At the time, more than 800 million people lacked enough food, and leaders pledged to halve that figure.

The plan sets out steps on trade, farm output, aid, and care for the poorest families. It asks states to treat access to food as a right and to act on it at home. Readers get the full 1990s blueprint for a world food fight, in the words states agreed.
un-ga-res-address-to-the-43rd-u-n-genera: Delegates at the forty-third session of the United Nations General Assembly in 1988 heard this formal address during the yearly general debate. Leaders used that debate to state their views before all member states. They spoke on war, peace, and world affairs. The speech belongs to a Cold War era that was nearing its end. Ties between East and West had begun to thaw.
un-un-res-fifth-progress-report-of-the-s:
Early 1999 in Sierra Leone is covered by the fifth progress report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission there, document S/1999/237. Weeks before, rebel forces had stormed the capital, Freetown, in a brutal January assault. The small observer mission, UNOMSIL, had to rebuild its work amid the wreckage.

The report describes the security crisis, harm to civilians, and steps to restore the elected government. It also covers aid needs and the mission's own staffing. The text is a snapshot of a peace effort under extreme strain, written for the Security Council.
un-un-res-first-progress-report-of-the-s:
A new observer mission in Sierra Leone gets its first progress report here, filed by the Secretary-General in 1998 as document S/1998/750. The Security Council had just created UNOMSIL to watch the country's shaky return to elected rule. Its military observers were few and lightly armed by design.

The report sets out the mission's first steps, its talks with the government, and the state of security on the ground. It flags rebel activity as the chief threat to peace. The document opens a run of reports that chart the mission's short, troubled life.
un-un-res-sixth-progress-report-of-the-s:
Spring 1999 in Sierra Leone fills the sixth progress report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission there, document S/1999/645. The capital, Freetown, was still scarred by the rebel assault of January that year. Peace talks were under way, but fighting had not fully stopped.

The report reviews the talks, the plight of civilians, and steps to rebuild state authority. It covers aid convoys, freed child soldiers, and the mission's own small staff of observers. The document sits between disaster and deal, which gives it value as a record of the war's turning point.
un-un-res-third-progress-report-of-the-s:
The close of 1998 in Sierra Leone is charted in the third progress report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission there, document S/1998/1176. UNOMSIL observers were spread across a country where rebel attacks were growing bolder. The elected government leaned heavily on West African troops for survival.

The report covers rebel raids, harm to civilians, and the slow work of rebuilding the army and police. It also describes aid needs as families fled fresh fighting. The warnings in this report proved grimly accurate when the capital was attacked weeks later.
un-un-res-united-nations-convention-to-c:
Dry lands losing their soil is the target of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, adopted in 1994. The treaty grew out of the Rio Earth Summit, where African states pressed hardest for action on drought. It is the main world pact on land decay, though it draws less notice than the climate treaty.

The text commits states to national plans against desert spread, with rich states pledging funds and skills. It stresses local farmers, herders, and women's groups as the front line. Readers get the full legal frame for a slow crisis that now touches every continent.
un-un-res-united-nations-millennium-decl:
World leaders adopted the Millennium Declaration at a United Nations summit in New York in September 2000. More heads of state and government gathered there than ever before. They used the turn of the century to state shared values and a shared to-do list for the world.

The declaration pledges action on poverty, disease, illiteracy, war, and harm to nature. It affirms freedom, equality, and respect for human rights as core values. Its targets were later turned into the Millennium Development Goals, which steered aid work for fifteen years. The text is the source document of that era.
united-states-presidents-inaugural-speec:
Inaugural Addresses of the Presidents of the United States collects the speeches from George Washington to George W. Bush, covering the years 1789 to 2005. The book opens with Washington's first address, given in New York City on Thursday, April 30, 1789. A note before the speech explains that he took his oath on the balcony of Federal Hall, that Chancellor Robert R. Livingston gave the oath, and that the Bible used belonged to a New York Masonic lodge.

Washington begins by telling the Senate and House that no event could have filled him with greater anxieties than his call to office. He speaks of leaving a retreat he had chosen with fond hopes, summoned by a country whose voice he hears with respect and love. Readers can follow how each later president used the same occasion to set out hopes, plans, and warnings at the start of a term.
veritables-clavicules-salomon:
Les Véritables Clavicules de Salomon, the True Keys of Solomon, is a French Solomonic grimoire dated about 1780. It stands apart from the Key tradition that Mathers later edited in English. This redaction carries its own catalog of spirits and its own arrangement of the rites.

French magicians thus worked from keys cut to another pattern. Seals, conjurations, and planetary hours follow the family's familiar forms with local differences. The book shows how the Solomonic corpus kept branching in manuscript and cheap print. Each region guarded its own version of Solomon's wisdom. For scholars, the Véritables Clavicules proves that the Key was never one book but a clan of them.
vestiges-of-the-natural-history-of-creat: Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation appeared at London in 1844. No author's name stands on the title page. Pages present here hold that title page and a full contents list, so the text itself is not shown. The contents march from the bodies of space and the making of the earth through the eras of rocks. Coal forests, reptiles, birds, and mammals follow. Closing chapters weigh the origin of living tribes. They set out a hypothesis for how the plant and animal kingdoms developed.
wage-earning-and-education: R. R. Lutz wrote Wage Earning and Education for the Cleveland Education Survey. The Survey Committee of the Cleveland Foundation issued it in 1916. Leonard P. Ayres directed the survey, and James R. Garfield served as the committee's counsel. Pages present here hold title pages only. They name the committee members and its chairman Charles E. Adams. The study itself, on how schooling meets the world of wages in Cleveland, is not shown. The title pages frame it as civic work: a foundation paying experts to measure a city's schools.
walter-sherwood-s-probation:
Horatio Alger Jr. opens Walter Sherwood's Probation in the plain library of Doctor Ezekiel Mack. His housekeeper, Miss Nancy Sprague, brings in a letter. She is a former schoolmistress who prides herself on her words, and she surmises the letter is from Walter. The doctor, rising sixty, is glad of his ward's care. Yet he answers that he wishes he felt as sure about the boy's head as about his heart.

The letter explains his worry. Walter writes from college that he is forced to ask again, so soon after his last. College life costs far more than he had supposed, and a fellow is expected to spend. Alger sets his pattern at once: a good-hearted youth in money trouble, under a kind guardian's eye. The probation of the title will test whether Walter's heart or his head rules him.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
Philemon is book 57 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Paul writes as a prisoner for Christ, with Timothy beside him. The note goes to Philemon, to Apphia, and to the church that meets in his house. Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith.

Then comes the plea at the heart of the note. Paul sends back Onesimus, a man once of no use and now of great use. Age and chains, Paul says, move him to appeal in love rather than give orders. Weymouth makes the short, tactful note easy to read and feel.

Revelation is book 66, the last in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. John says the reveal came from Christ through an angel, to show what must soon take place. A blessing rests on those who read and keep the words. The time, John warns, is close at hand.

Greetings go to seven churches in the province of Asia. Christ is praised as the first of the dead to rise and the ruler of kings. He will come with the clouds, and all eyes will see him. John calls himself a brother who shares in sorrow and patience. Weymouth gives the vision in clear, grave words.
wieland-oberon:
Christoph Martin Wieland retold the medieval tale of Huon of Bordeaux in Oberon, the great verse romance of the German Enlightenment. The fairy king Oberon guides the hero through trials, magic, and love in this German text from Project Gutenberg. Wit and sensibility replace the old epic's rough edges.

Charming, polished, and quietly sensual, the poem became the most popular German poem of its age. Goethe praised it, and Weber later turned its world into a beloved opera. Wieland's couplets move with a lightness German verse had rarely achieved. A landmark of German literature, the poem reads best in the original, as here. Its blend of fairy tale and feeling captures the Enlightenment learning to dream again.
will-warburton:
George Gissing opens Will Warburton with his hero just back from Alpine snows. Warburton springs from a cab near Chelsea Bridge, pays double fare, and runs up four flights with a heavy bag. His landlady, Mrs. Hopper, peers through a narrow crack of the door. He greets her warmly and begs dinner in three minutes.

After a wash, he tears through a pile of letters with grunts and laughs. Dinner is a noble steak, an apple tart, cheddar, and two bottles of Bass, gone in a quarter hour. Warburton is a hearty man near thirty, full of force. Gissing sets up a tale of a gentleman turned grocer, and pride under strain.
winds-of-doctrine-studies-in-contemporar:
G. Santayana wrote Winds of Doctrine, studies in the thought of his day, first printed by Scribner in 1913. Santayana had lately been a professor of philosophy at Harvard. His contents take up the temper of the age, modernism and Christianity, and the thought of Henri Bergson. Bertrand Russell gets a long study in four parts. Shelley and the genteel tradition in America close the set.

The first essay calls the present age a critical one, worth living in. The old civilization of Christendom has not vanished, Santayana says, yet a new one has begun to take its place. Old and new still overlap and can be compared. Readers meet a calm, clear critic sorting the ideas of his time.
windy-mcpherson-s-son:
Sherwood Anderson wrote Windy McPherson's Son, a novel of a small Iowa town. Sam McPherson, thirteen, tall and big-boned, steps onto the Caxton station platform at dusk. He walks with care on the hot, cracked boards in his bare feet. A bundle of newspapers rides under one arm, and a long black cigar sits in his hand.

Jerry Donlin, the baggage man, laughs at the cigar and winks. Sam hands it over and gives brisk orders like a born trader. He then counts on his fingers as he walks toward main street. Anderson gave the book to the men and women of his own midwestern home town. A boy's rise and a father's shadow drive the tale.
with-rimington:
L. March Phillipps, late captain in Rimington's Guides, wrote With Rimington about the South African war. Edward Arnold printed the second impression in London in 1902. His dedication honors Lieutenant Gustavus Coulson, a friend from childhood who fell in May 1901. Coulson rallied men and saved a gun at Lambrechtfontein, then died bringing off a wounded man under fire.

That deed, the colonel wrote, won a recommendation for the Victoria Cross. The two men had ridden together from Lindley toward Pretoria, talking of Devon home. Phillipps calls him the type of the gallant boys who died for England in that war. Letters from the march make up the book. Memory and loss frame the campaign tales.
with-the-immortal-seventh-division: Only the title page is present here for With the Immortal Seventh Division, so the chaplain's account does not appear. The Reverend E. J. Kennedy, a chaplain major with the expeditionary force, wrote the book. The Lord Bishop of Winchester supplied a preface, by the title page's note. Hodder and Stoughton printed it in London, New York, and Toronto in 1916. A transcriber's note says each chapter was preceded by blank and title pages in the original. The division's name promises a tale of Great War service.
with-the-procession:
Henry B. Fuller wrote this novel about David Marshall, a rich Chicago wholesale grocer. The opening shows Marshall's family treating him like a money machine. They know his head and hands, yet they never think of him as a full person. When he takes to his bed, they feel surprise and impatience more than pity.

The story then steps back to a city scene at a drawbridge. A tug pulls a schooner toward lumber yards while carts and a streetcar wait to cross. Readers get a family portrait set inside a busy trading city. Money, duty, and feeling pull against each other from the start.
woman-as-decoration: Emily Burbank wrote this illustrated guide to dress and appearance, published in New York in 1917. Pages present here hold the title page, a dedication, and a description of the first plate. That plate sketches opera singer Geraldine Farrar as Thais, in a gilded wig and rich gown. The caption explains the costume follows accounts of the real Thais of Alexandria. No chapter text appears in these pages, so Burbank's advice itself stays unseen here.
